subtypes.distinguishing_features: A finding included among factors that may raise concern for GCNIS, especially with other risks.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify TM and assess for associated lesions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Testicular imaging or evaluation of associated risk factors.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: TM alone does not establish malignancy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate GCNIS in selected higher-risk men.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be offered to infertile men with TM and higher-risk features; suspicious associated findings require discussion of invasive assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess suspicious findings and choose among surveillance, biopsy or orchidectomy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: TM with an associated lesion or other concerning findings.

follow_up.schedule: Regular self-examination is advised, including for men without additional risk factors; a specific imaging schedule is not established for higher-risk men.
long_term_effects: Higher testicular cancer risk in infertile men with TM.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: For isolated TM without associated risk factors, the guideline advises against testicular biopsy, follow-up scrotal US, biochemical tumour markers and abdominal or pelvic computed tomography.

conditions.name: Varicocele
conditions.description: A common congenital venous abnormality that can be associated with impaired testicular growth, sub-fertility, discomfort or hypogonadism.
conditions.epidemiology: Present in almost 15% of the general male population, 25% of men with abnormal semen analysis and 35-40% of men presenting with infertility. Reported incidence is 35–44% in primary infertility and 45–81% in secondary infertility.
conditions.clinical_presentation: It may be palpable or visible, cause pain or discomfort, and accompany abnormal semen parameters. Worsening semen parameters are associated with greater grade and age.

subtypes.name: Subclinical
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Neither palpable nor visible at rest or with Valsalva manoeuvre, but detectable with a special test such as Doppler US.

subtypes.name: Grade 1
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Palpable during Valsalva manoeuvre.

subtypes.name: Grade 2
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Palpable at rest.

subtypes.name: Grade 3
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Visible and palpable at rest.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the clinical diagnosis and grade.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Palpability and visibility at rest or during Valsalva manoeuvre distinguish the stated grades.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess reflux, vein diameter and persistent or recurrent varicocele.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Inconclusive examination or persistently unsatisfactory semen analysis after repair.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A maximum diameter > 3 mm while upright and during Valsalva manoeuvre, together with reflux lasting > 2 seconds, correlates with clinically significant varicocele.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess fertility-related semen abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Infertility evaluation or assessment after repair.

diagnostic_workup.test: Testicular volume assessment using Lambert’s formula
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate volume in patients with infertility and/or varicocele.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The stated formula is V=L x W x H x 0.71.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate underlying pathology or congenital anomalies.
Assess DNA damage when relevant to infertility or ART failure.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Evaluation of selected men with infertility, particularly after ART failure or recurrent pregnancy loss.

definitions.description: Detected by a special examination but not palpable or visible at rest or during Valsalva manoeuvre.
Both visible and palpable at rest.

follow_up.schedule: After adolescent treatment decisions, persistent testicular size differences are confirmed at two subsequent visits six months apart; after repair, semen improvement generally takes up to two spermatogenic cycles.
recommended_tests: Serial clinical or Doppler US assessment of adolescent testicular growth when indicated.
Semen analysis after repair when results remain unsatisfactory.
Scrotal Doppler US when persistence or recurrence is suspected.
long_term_effects: Potential progressive testicular damage and reduced fertility.

conditions.name: Male accessory gland infections (MAGIs)
conditions.description: Infections affecting the male urogenital tract; the WHO groups urethritis, prostatitis, orchitis and epididymitis under this designation. Their effect on semen quality and natural conception is not firmly established.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Infection may be symptomatic or asymptomatic. Leukocytospermia indicates inflammation but does not reliably establish bacterial or viral infection.

subtypes.name: Epididymitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Typically causes acute unilateral epididymal pain and swelling.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess sperm quality and possible prostatic involvement.

diagnostic_workup.test: Semen culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify common urinary-tract pathogens.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A concentration of urinary tract pathogens > 103 CFU/mL in ejaculate indicates significant bacteriospermia; the sample should reach the laboratory the same day.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm leukocytospermia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: After excluding UTI, including urethritis, > 106 peroxidase-positive WBCs/mL of ejaculate indicates inflammation; the stated WHO leukocytospermia definition is > 106 WBCs/mL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect the organism in semen.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document identifies PCR as the most accurate available method, while stating that an ideal diagnostic test has not been established.

conditions.name: Epididymitis
conditions.description: Inflammation of the epididymis that can arise from sexually transmitted infection or be associated with urinary-tract infection.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Usually presents with acute unilateral pain and swelling. In sexually active men aged < 35 years, C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoea are the most frequent cited causes; non-sexually transmitted cases occur more often at > 35 years.

subtypes.name: Sexually transmitted epididymitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Usually accompanies urethritis.

subtypes.name: Non-sexually transmitted epididymitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Associated with UTIs and more common in men aged > 35 years.

diagnostic_workup.test: Ejaculate analysis according to WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (6th edn) criteria
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess persistent inflammation and semen changes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Sperm counts and progressive motility can decline transiently.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help identify pathogenic organisms.

recommended_tests: Ejaculate analysis when assessing persistent inflammation or fertility effects.
long_term_effects: Bilateral disease can be followed by epididymal-duct stenosis, reduced sperm count or azoospermia.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: For known or suspected N. gonorrhoeae or C. trachomatis infection, sexual partners should be referred for evaluation and treatment.

conditions.name: Secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism
conditions.description: An endocrine cause of impaired fertility involving insufficient gonadotrophin stimulation; hyperprolactinaemia may suppress gonadotrophins and contribute to sub-fertility.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May present with impaired spermatogenesis or sub-fertility.

subtypes.name: Prepubertal secondary hypogonadism
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline distinguishes this form from post-pubertal onset in its discussion of fertility treatment.

subtypes.name: Post-Pubertal Onset
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline describes stimulation of spermatogenesis with hCG, with FSH added or used from the outset when appropriate.

subtypes.name: Secondary hypogonadism due to hyperprolactinemia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Elevated prolactin suppresses gonadotrophins; a pituitary adenoma or a causative drug may be involved.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Classify hypogonadism and assess testicular function.
Identify a potentially treatable cause of gonadotrophin suppression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected secondary hypogonadism related to elevated prolactin.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform expectations for response to gonadotrophin treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Greater baseline testicular volume is described as a favourable prognostic indicator.

follow_up.schedule: During the described post-pubertal hCG treatment, semen analysis is performed every 3 months unless conception occurs.
recommended_tests: Semen analysis every 3 months during the described treatment.
Testosterone assessment during hCG dose adjustment.

conditions.name: Primary Hypogonadism
conditions.description: Testicular deficiency commonly accompanied by increased FSH and LH, with or without low testosterone.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Impaired spermatogenesis may accompany testicular failure; FSH commonly rises when spermatogonia are absent or markedly reduced.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and classify testicular deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected hypogonadism or infertility with testicular dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: FSH and LH are usually elevated, while testosterone may or may not be low. Normal FSH does not exclude maturation arrest.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate testicular deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Normal volume does not reliably rule out maturation arrest or predict sperm retrieval.

conditions.name: Ejaculatory duct obstruction (EDO)
conditions.description: A distal seminal-tract obstruction that may be post-inflammatory, cystic or associated with other ejaculatory-duct abnormalities.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Low semen volume, acidic pH and severe oligozoospermia or azoospermia can raise suspicion of distal obstruction.

subtypes.name: Post-inflammatory obstruction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Obstruction follows inflammation.

subtypes.name: Cystic obstruction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A cyst, including a midline intraprostatic cyst, contributes to the blockage.

diagnostic_workup.test: Semen analysis, including volume and pH
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a pattern compatible with distal obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Low volume and acidic pH with severe oligozoospermia or azoospermia support further assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify complete or partial obstruction and associated duct or seminal-vesicle abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected partial or complete distal obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Potential findings include ejaculatory-duct cysts, seminal-vesicle dilatation, hypoplasia or atrophy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate a differential diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected distal obstruction, particularly with low semen volume.

conditions.name: Leukocytospermia
conditions.description: An elevated concentration of white blood cells in ejaculate that indicates inflammation but does not necessarily indicate bacterial or viral infection.
conditions.clinical_presentation: It can occur without symptoms of a genital-tract infection.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify increased leukocytes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Semen assessment or suspected genital inflammation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The stated WHO definition is > 106 WBCs/mL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm leukocytospermia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Increased leukocytes are detected in ejaculate.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Leukocytospermia alone is not a reliable indicator of infection.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish other sources of urinary or genital inflammation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Interpretation of increased peroxidase-positive cells in ejaculate.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with elevated SDF in ejaculated sperm after unsuccessful ART.
decision_rules: Consider testicular sperm for ICSI only on an individual basis after discussion with reproductive specialists.
Before considering TESE, address varicoceles, dietary and lifestyle factors, accessory gland infections and abstinence time, and account for female-partner factors.

alternative_regimens.name: TESE-ICSI
alternative_regimens.summary: Testicular sperm may be considered for ICSI as an experimental approach after ART failure.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: High SDF in ejaculated sperm after assessment of potentially correctable factors and discussion of the risks of an invasive procedure.

supportive_care: Explain that evidence is limited and live-birth rates are under-reported.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A possible advantage has not been confirmed in large-scale RCTs; the benefit in cryptozoospermia or oligozoospermia is also unconfirmed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with Klinefelter syndrome and azoospermia who wish to pursue fertility treatment.
decision_rules: Offer surgical sperm retrieval as a fertility-treatment option.
Address fertility before considering testosterone therapy for testosterone levels in the hypogonadal range.

recommended_regimens.name: TESE
recommended_regimens.summary: Surgically retrieve testicular sperm in azoospermic men.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Spermatozoa can be recovered in up to 50% of cases.

alternative_regimens.name: mTESE
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative surgical method for retrieving testicular sperm.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Azoospermia in a man with Klinefelter syndrome.

supportive_care: Provide long-term endocrine follow-up and appropriate medical care.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Some evidence suggests better sperm recovery at younger ages, but no age threshold is established.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pre-pubertal or peri-pubertal boys, and older boys who have not considered their fertility potential.
decision_rules: Limit sperm retrieval intended for fertility preservation in these groups to research settings.

not_recommended.name: Testicular sperm extraction for cryopreservation outside a research setting
not_recommended.reason: This approach remains experimental in pre-pubertal or peri-pubertal boys; the same restriction applies to older boys who have not considered their fertility potential.

treatment_pathways.condition: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with CBAVD-only or CF seeking pregnancy.
decision_rules: Use surgically aspirated or extracted sperm with ICSI when pursuing pregnancy.
Test the female partner for CF mutations and counsel the couple about reproductive risk before ICSI.

recommended_regimens.name: MESA and ICSI
recommended_regimens.summary: Obtain epididymal sperm microsurgically for use with ICSI.

recommended_regimens.name: PESA and ICSI
recommended_regimens.summary: Obtain epididymal sperm percutaneously for use with ICSI.

alternative_regimens.name: TESA and ICSI
alternative_regimens.summary: Use aspirated testicular sperm with ICSI.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative source of sperm in CBAVD-only or CF.

alternative_regimens.name: TESE and ICSI
alternative_regimens.summary: Use extracted testicular sperm with ICSI.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative source of sperm in CBAVD-only or CF.

supportive_care: Provide genetic counselling when CFTR mutations are identified.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Compared with CF patients, those with CBAVD-only have been reported to have better sperm quality, easier retrieval and better ICSI outcomes. If the female partner carries CFTR mutations, the stated risk of a child with CF or CBAVD is 50%, depending on the parental mutations.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with complete deletions involving AZFa and AZFb who are being considered for testicular sperm retrieval.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: Complete deletions that include the AZFa and AZFb regions
decision_rules: Do not proceed with surgical testicular sperm retrieval when these complete deletions are present.

not_recommended.name: TESE
not_recommended.reason: Complete deletions involving AZFa and AZFb have a very poor prognosis for sperm retrieval; the guideline describes the chance of retrieval as almost zero.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Post-pubertal men with cryptorchidism.
decision_rules: Do not use hormonal therapy to induce testicular descent after puberty.

not_recommended.name: Human chorionic gonadotropin
not_recommended.reason: Hormonal treatment is not recommended for cryptorchidism in adulthood.

not_recommended.name: GnRH
not_recommended.reason: Hormonal treatment is not recommended for cryptorchidism in adulthood.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adult men with a unilateral palpable undescended testis and normal hormonal function and spermatogenesis in the contralateral testis.
decision_rules: Offer removal of the undescended testis when the opposite testis functions normally.

recommended_regimens.name: orchidectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer removal of the unilateral undescended testis because of its risk of GCNIS and subsequent GCT.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Regular self-examination of the undescended testis is not an option in this population.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adult men with unilateral or bilateral undescended testes and biochemical hypogonadism or spermatogenic failure.
decision_rules: Offer unilateral or bilateral testicular repositioning when technically feasible to preserve androgen production and fertility.
If an undescended testis is corrected in adulthood, perform a biopsy during the operation to assess for GCNIS.

recommended_regimens.name: orchidopexy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer unilateral or bilateral surgery when contralateral function is impaired or fertility preservation is important.

recommended_regimens.name: testicular biopsy
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform biopsy when correcting an undescended testis in adulthood to detect intratubular GCNIS.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Adult correction of bilateral cryptorchidism may permit sperm production in men previously diagnosed with azoospermia. Vascular injury during orchidopexy can cause testicular atrophy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adolescents with an intra-abdominal undescended testis and a normal contralateral testis.
decision_rules: Removal of the intra-abdominal testis can be recommended because of malignancy risk.

recommended_regimens.name: orchidectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider removing the intra-abdominal undescended testis when the opposite testis is normal.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with testicular cancer before planned orchidectomy or potentially gonadotoxic or ablative cancer treatment.
decision_rules: Offer fertility-preservation counselling and sperm cryopreservation before treatment that may impair spermatogenesis or ejaculation.
Assess semen before orchidectomy to identify men who might benefit from surgical sperm retrieval.
Do not delay orchidectomy unduly when cryopreservation facilities are unavailable or preservation would delay treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: sperm cryopreservation
recommended_regimens.summary: Preserve ejaculated sperm before planned orchidectomy or additional oncological treatment when feasible.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Before planned orchidectomy or neoadjuvant or adjuvant oncological therapies

alternative_regimens.name: c/mTESE
alternative_regimens.summary: Surgically obtain sperm for preservation if ejaculated sperm preservation is not feasible.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia identified before orchidectomy.

response_assessment.interpretation: Identify azoospermia or severe abnormalities that may warrant concurrent sperm retrieval.

supportive_care: Provide fertility-preservation counselling before gonadotoxic treatment.
Use contraception during chemotherapy and RT and for at least six months after completion.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document states that a harmful effect on survival from cryopreservation-related treatment delay has not been investigated.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with testicular cancer and azoospermia or severe semen-parameter abnormalities who undergo radical orchidectomy.
decision_rules: Offer surgical sperm retrieval at the time of orchidectomy.

recommended_regimens.name: onco-TESE
recommended_regimens.summary: Extract and preserve testicular sperm during radical orchidectomy.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At the time of radical orchidectomy

supportive_care: Arrange access to a urologist experienced in TESE.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men previously treated for TGCT.
decision_rules: Provide multidisciplinary survivorship care addressing endocrine, sexual and cardiovascular effects.
When fertility remains a priority, weigh testosterone therapy against its potential to worsen spermatogenesis.

recommended_regimens.name: survivorship program
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide multidisciplinary follow-up through a dedicated late-effects service.

alternative_regimens.name: clomiphene
alternative_regimens.summary: An off-label option to consider instead of testosterone therapy when preserving fertility is important.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Symptoms suggestive of TDS in a patient who places high value on fertility potential.

alternative_regimens.name: hCG
alternative_regimens.summary: An off-label gonadotrophin-analogue option in this setting.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Symptoms suggestive of TDS when the patient prioritises fertility potential.

response_assessment.interpretation: Assess for hypogonadism; the reported risk is greatest at 6-12 months post-treatment.

supportive_care: Assess sexual dysfunction, cardiovascular risk, and psychological and social needs.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document considers it reasonable to defer testosterone therapy until signs or symptoms of testosterone deficiency persist.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with isolated TM and no associated risk factors for testicular cancer.
decision_rules: Advise regular testicular self-examination.
Do not pursue invasive investigation or imaging surveillance solely for isolated TM.

recommended_regimens.name: testicular self-examination
recommended_regimens.summary: Advise self-examination to facilitate early recognition of a possible TGCT.

not_recommended.name: testicular biopsy
not_recommended.reason: Isolated TM without additional risk factors does not warrant biopsy.

not_recommended.name: follow-up scrotal ultrasound
not_recommended.reason: Routine imaging surveillance is not indicated for isolated TM without additional risk factors.

not_recommended.name: biochemical tumour markers
not_recommended.reason: Measurement is not indicated for isolated TM without additional risk factors.

not_recommended.name: abdominal or pelvic computed tomography
not_recommended.reason: Imaging is not indicated for isolated TM without additional risk factors.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document states that testicular cancer does not develop in most men with asymptomatic TM.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Infertile men with TM and higher-risk features, including spermatogenic failure, bilateral TM, atrophic testes (< 12 mL), a history of undescended testes or TGCT.
decision_rules: Offer biopsy after explaining its risks and complications.
If examination or US identifies an associated suspicious lesion, decide among surgical exploration with biopsy and orchidectomy through multidisciplinary discussion with the patient.

recommended_regimens.name: testicular biopsy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer biopsy to infertile men with TM who have the specified higher-risk characteristics.

alternative_regimens.name: inguinal surgical exploration with testicular biopsy
alternative_regimens.summary: Investigate an associated suspicious lesion surgically.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Suspicious physical examination or US findings after multidisciplinary and patient discussion.

alternative_regimens.name: orchidectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer removal as an option for an associated suspicious lesion.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Suspicious physical examination or US findings after multidisciplinary and patient discussion.

supportive_care: Explain the risks and complications of biopsy.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation to undertake surgical exploration with biopsy or offer orchidectomy for suspicious associated lesions has a Strong rating.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Infertile men with a clinical varicocele and abnormal semen parameters whose infertility is otherwise unexplained, when the female partner has good ovarian reserve.
decision_rules: Treat a clinically evident varicocele in this population to improve fertility rates.
Discuss the female partner’s ovarian reserve and the interval before expected improvement when choosing intervention.

recommended_regimens.name: varicocele repair
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat a clinical varicocele associated with abnormal semen findings and otherwise unexplained infertility.

recommended_regimens.name: microsurgical varicocelectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: The document identifies the microsurgical approach as the most effective of the described varicocelectomy techniques.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A Cochrane review reported a slightly greater pregnancy rate with microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy than with other surgical treatments (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.36).

alternative_regimens.name: sclerotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: A minimally invasive radiological treatment option.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choice of intervention after considering recurrence, complications and available expertise.

alternative_regimens.name: embolisation
alternative_regimens.summary: A minimally invasive radiological treatment option.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choice of intervention after considering recurrence, complications and available expertise.

response_assessment.timepoint: Up to two spermatogenic cycles after treatment
response_assessment.interpretation: This is the average period reported for improvement.

supportive_care: Counsel about surgical risks, recurrence and the possibility of hydrocele.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document reports spontaneous pregnancy between 6 and 12 months after varicocelectomy. It also states that large prospective RCTs comparing the interventions are unavailable.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Infertile men with normal semen analysis or men with a sub-clinical varicocele.
decision_rules: Do not treat varicocele in either group.

not_recommended.name: varicocele treatment
not_recommended.reason: The guideline strongly advises against treatment when semen analysis is normal or the varicocele is sub-clinical; studies cited in the document did not show a benefit for these groups.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adolescents with varicocele and a persistently smaller testis.
decision_rules: Offer surgery when the testicular size difference is > 2 mL or 20% and persists across two subsequent visits performed six months apart.
Avoid prophylactic intervention without documented testicular growth deterioration or abnormal semen analysis because of overtreatment risk.

recommended_regimens.name: surgery for varicocele
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer intervention for confirmed, persistent testicular size disparity.

not_recommended.name: prophylactic varicocelectomy without documented deterioration
not_recommended.reason: Most adolescents with a varicocele do not later experience difficulty achieving pregnancy, creating a substantial risk of overtreatment.

response_assessment.timepoint: Two subsequent visits performed six months apart
response_assessment.interpretation: Confirm that a size difference of > 2 mL or 20% persists.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with clinical varicocele, raised SDF and otherwise unexplained infertility or previous ART failure, including recurrent pregnancy loss or failure of embryogenesis or implantation.
decision_rules: Varicocelectomy may be considered after assessing other causes of elevated SDF and counselling the couple.
Take account of the female partner’s ovarian reserve, operative risks and potential delay to ART, particularly when standard semen parameters are normal.

alternative_regimens.name: varicocelectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: An intervention that may be considered for elevated sperm DNA damage with otherwise unexplained infertility or ART failure.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individualised decision after evaluation of other contributors to SDF and discussion with the couple.

response_assessment.interpretation: A systematic review and meta-analysis associated varicocelectomy with lower postoperative SDF.

supportive_care: Discuss the potential delay to ART and operative risks.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: This recommendation has a Weak rating. Whether intervention is warranted when SDF is raised but conventional semen parameters are normal remains uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with NOA and a clinically significant varicocele.
decision_rules: Discuss possible varicocele repair only after explaining the low quality of the available evidence and weighing its risks and benefits.

alternative_regimens.name: varicocelectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: Repair may allow sperm to appear in the ejaculate and could avoid a subsequent retrieval procedure.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individualised consideration in NOA with a clinical varicocele.

response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether sperm have appeared in the ejaculate.

supportive_care: Explain the uncertainty of benefit before intervention.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In the cited meta-analyses, postoperative ejaculate contained sperm in 43.9% of patients (range: 20.8%-55.0%); the evidence quality was low.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with male accessory gland infections.
decision_rules: Treat the infection because sperm quality may improve, while explaining that conception is not necessarily more likely.
If a sexually transmitted cause is known or suspected, refer sexual partners for evaluation and treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: treatment of male accessory gland infections
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat an identified infection for its possible sperm-quality benefit without presenting improved conception as established.

supportive_care: Refer sexual partners for assessment and treatment when a sexually transmitted disease is known or suspected.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The partner-referral recommendation has a Strong rating. The document provides no infection-specific antibiotic regimen here.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with chronic bacterial prostatitis classified as NIH II.
decision_rules: Use antibiotics for the documented infection and symptoms, without assuming that treatment increases natural conception.

recommended_regimens.name: antibiotic therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat NIH II chronic bacterial prostatitis; the document reports symptomatic relief and eradication of microorganisms.

response_assessment.interpretation: Assess relief and eradication of microorganisms.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Although antibiotics might improve sperm quality, the document says there is no evidence that treatment of CP/CPPS increases the probability of natural conception.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with epididymitis known or suspected to be caused by N. gonorrhoeae or C. trachomatis.
decision_rules: Treat the infection and tell the patient that sexual partners also need evaluation and treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: treatment of epididymitis
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat to resolve the infection and symptoms and reduce testicular damage, transmission and complications.

response_assessment.interpretation: Consider persistent inflammation, reduced sperm count, azoospermia or epididymal duct stenosis.

supportive_care: Direct sexual partners for evaluation and treatment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No pathogen-specific antibiotic regimen is specified.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Infertile men with lifestyle factors that may impair fertility.
decision_rules: Counsel about obesity, limited physical activity, smoking and high alcohol intake, and advise improvements to increase the chance of conception.

recommended_regimens.name: life-style changes
recommended_regimens.summary: Advise weight management, increased physical activity, smoking cessation and reduced alcohol intake as applicable.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence on weight loss and semen quality is conflicting across study designs; the cited meta-analysis did not find improved sperm quality or function after bariatric surgery in morbidly obese men.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with idiopathic infertility being considered for empirical supplements or endocrine agents.
decision_rules: Do not routinely prescribe the listed empirical treatments because their benefit is not conclusive.

not_recommended.name: antioxidants
not_recommended.reason: Routine use is discouraged because evidence of benefit in idiopathic infertility is inconclusive.

not_recommended.name: prebiotic/probiotic
not_recommended.reason: Routine use is discouraged because evidence of benefit in idiopathic infertility is inconclusive.

not_recommended.name: selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs)
not_recommended.reason: Routine use is discouraged because the available evidence does not support a conclusive recommendation.

not_recommended.name: aromatase inhibitors (AIs)
not_recommended.reason: Routine use is discouraged because the available evidence does not support a conclusive recommendation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation against routine use has a Weak rating. The document reports differing trial and review findings rather than an established absence of benefit.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with post-pubertal-onset secondary hypogonadism who wish to induce spermatogenesis.
decision_rules: Usually begin with hCG alone; add FSH if spermatogenesis is not stimulated.
Starting hCG and FSH together is another option.

recommended_regimens.name: hCG
recommended_regimens.summary: Use gonadotrophin-based therapy to induce spermatogenesis in a man seeking conception. The suggested starting dose is 250 IU hCG twice weekly; if testosterone becomes normal, the dose may be increased up to 2,000 IU twice weekly.

alternative_regimens.name: FSH and hCG
alternative_regimens.summary: Combination treatment can begin at treatment initiation; FSH can also be added after inadequate stimulation with hCG alone at 75 IU three times per week, increasing to 150 IU three times per week if indicated.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An initial combination strategy or failure to stimulate spermatogenesis with hCG alone.

response_assessment.timepoint: Every 3 months unless conception has occurred

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Greater baseline testicular volume is a favourable prognostic indicator. The document reports no outcome difference between urinary-derived, highly purified FSH and recombinant FSH.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with congenital or acquired hypogonadotropic hypogonadism who wish to conceive.
decision_rules: Induce spermatogenesis with effective gonadotrophin-based drug treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: hCG
recommended_regimens.summary: A recommended drug option for induction of spermatogenesis.

recommended_regimens.name: human menopausal gonadotropins
recommended_regimens.summary: A recommended drug option for induction of spermatogenesis.

recommended_regimens.name: recombinant FSH
recommended_regimens.summary: A recommended drug option for induction of spermatogenesis.

recommended_regimens.name: highly purified FSH
recommended_regimens.summary: A recommended drug option for induction of spermatogenesis.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For prepubertal secondary hypogonadism, the evidence summary describes FSH with hCG or pulsatile GnRH; use of pulsatile GnRH is limited by difficult administration.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with proven hyperprolactinaemia causing gonadotrophin suppression and subfertility.
decision_rules: Treat with a dopamine agonist or withdraw the causative drug when applicable; the approach applies irrespective of the cause, including pituitary adenoma.

recommended_regimens.name: dopamine agonist therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer treatment to improve sperm quality in proven hyperprolactinemia.

alternative_regimens.name: bromocriptine
alternative_regimens.summary: A named dopamine agonist option.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Hyperprolactinaemia requiring dopamine agonist therapy.

alternative_regimens.name: cabergoline
alternative_regimens.summary: A named dopamine agonist option.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Hyperprolactinaemia requiring dopamine agonist therapy.

alternative_regimens.name: quinagolide
alternative_regimens.summary: A named dopamine agonist option.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Hyperprolactinaemia requiring dopamine agonist therapy.

alternative_regimens.name: withdrawal of the causative drug
alternative_regimens.summary: Stop a medication responsible for hyperprolactinaemia.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A drug is identified as the cause.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with idiopathic oligozoospermia and FSH values within the normal range.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: FSH levels within the normal range (generally 1.5 – 8 mIU/mL)
decision_rules: FSH treatment may be used to increase spermatogenesis; do not treat idiopathic infertility with high dose FSH.

recommended_regimens.name: FSH
recommended_regimens.summary: Use FSH for idiopathic oligozoospermia when baseline FSH is normal.

not_recommended.name: high dose FSH
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against its use for idiopathic infertility; evidence is insufficient to support routine high-dose treatment.

response_assessment.interpretation: Assess spermatogenic response; no assessment interval is specified.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Studies cited by the document reported improvements in semen parameters and SDF, but treatment protocols and findings varied.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Infertile men with classical primary testicular failure who seek improved spermatogenesis.
decision_rules: Do not assume that gonadotrophin therapy or other hormonal agents improve spermatogenesis in classical testicular failure.

not_recommended.name: gonadotrophin therapy
not_recommended.reason: There is no substantial evidence of benefit in classical testicular failure.

not_recommended.name: SERMs
not_recommended.reason: The document identifies no supporting data for improved spermatogenesis in primary hypogonadism.

not_recommended.name: AIs
not_recommended.reason: The document identifies no supporting data for improved spermatogenesis in primary hypogonadism.

not_recommended.name: testosterone therapy for male infertility
not_recommended.reason: Testosterone therapy is contraindicated in infertile men and is not a treatment for male infertility.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation not to use testosterone therapy for male infertility has a Strong rating. Testosterone therapy is recommended for symptomatic primary or secondary hypogonadism when parenthood is not being considered.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Infertile men with oligospermia or azoospermia attributed to anabolic steroid abuse.
decision_rules: First withdraw anabolic steroids and allow time for sperm production to recover before considering stimulation.

recommended_regimens.name: withdrawal of anabolic steroids
recommended_regimens.summary: Stop the causative steroids before considering treatment to induce spermatogenesis.

response_assessment.timepoint: six to twelve months after cessation
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether recovery has occurred or infertility persists.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document states that management is based on case reports and clinical experience.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men whose impaired spermatogenesis persists after anabolic steroid withdrawal.
decision_rules: If recovery has not occurred after the withdrawal interval, consider drug treatment to stimulate spermatogenesis.

alternative_regimens.name: hCG
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used to stimulate spermatogenesis, either alone or with FSH.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent oligospermia or azoospermia after six to twelve months without anabolic steroids.

alternative_regimens.name: hCG and FSH
alternative_regimens.summary: A combination option for stimulating spermatogenesis.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent impairment after six to twelve months of steroid withdrawal.

alternative_regimens.name: clomiphene
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative option discussed for persistent impairment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent impairment after six to twelve months of steroid withdrawal.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document gives no standard indication or regimen for this situation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with intratesticular obstruction who require sperm for assisted reproduction.
decision_rules: Use testicular sperm retrieval because sperm cannot be extracted through the obstructed tract by another retrieval site.

recommended_regimens.name: testicular sperm retrieval
recommended_regimens.summary: Retrieve sperm directly from the testis in intratesticular obstruction.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with acquired epididymal obstruction whose female partners have good ovarian reserve.
decision_rules: Offer microsurgical reconstruction when the obstruction can be repaired.
Retrieve and cryopreserve sperm during reconstruction, particularly if reconstruction proves impossible.

recommended_regimens.name: microsurgical epididymovasostomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Reconstruct the epididymal outflow tract when the female partner has good ovarian reserve.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reported patency rates range between 63% and 85%, and cumulative natural pregnancy rates between 21% and 45%.

alternative_regimens.name: MESA/TESE and ICSI
alternative_regimens.summary: Retrieve sperm during surgery, cryopreserve it and use it for subsequent ICSI.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Reconstruction is impossible, or sperm preservation is undertaken as an adjunct to reconstruction.

response_assessment.interpretation: Recanalisation may take this long; a systematic review reported time to patency between 2.8 to 6.6 months.

supportive_care: Cryopreserve sperm retrieved intra-operatively for possible later ICSI.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Reported late failure after epididymovasostomy varies between 1 and 50% across heterogeneous reports.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with vas deferens obstruction after vasectomy and female partners with good ovarian reserve.
decision_rules: Offer microsurgical vasectomy reversal.
If findings in proximal vas fluid suggest secondary epididymal obstruction, consider epididymovasostomy.

recommended_regimens.name: microsurgical vasovasostomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Reverse vasectomy-associated vasal obstruction.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Mean post-procedural patency and pregnancy rates weighted by sample size were 90-97% and 52-73%, respectively.

alternative_regimens.name: microsurgical EV
alternative_regimens.summary: Reconstruct epididymal outflow if secondary epididymal obstruction is suspected.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No spermatozoa in intra-operative vas fluid, particularly when proximal fluid has a thick appearance.

alternative_regimens.name: robot-assisted vasovasostomy
alternative_regimens.summary: A technique with similar reported success rates; larger studies and cost-benefit analysis are needed.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available alternative to standard microsurgical reversal.

response_assessment.interpretation: This is the reported average time to patency.

supportive_care: Discuss simultaneous sperm retrieval and cryopreservation for possible future ICSI.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Reported late failures are uncommon (0-12%).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with obstruction unsuitable for reconstruction, limited ovarian reserve in the female partner, or a preference for proceeding directly to ICSI.
decision_rules: Use sperm retrieval rather than reconstruction when repair is not feasible or the couple chooses direct ICSI.
Sperm retrieval may also accompany reconstructive surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: MESA
recommended_regimens.summary: Retrieve epididymal sperm for use with ICSI.

recommended_regimens.name: TESE
recommended_regimens.summary: Retrieve testicular sperm for use with ICSI.

recommended_regimens.name: PESA
recommended_regimens.summary: Retrieve epididymal sperm percutaneously for use with ICSI.

recommended_regimens.name: TESA
recommended_regimens.summary: Retrieve testicular sperm percutaneously for use with ICSI.

supportive_care: Cryopreserve retrieved sperm when intended for later ICSI.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document reports comparable ICSI pregnancy outcomes with epididymal and testicular sperm in OA, but characterises the supporting studies as low-evidence.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with large bilateral inguinal vas deferens defects that cannot be corrected.
decision_rules: Use sperm retrieval and cryopreservation for future ICSI when reconstruction is not possible.

recommended_regimens.name: TESE/MESA/ PESA
recommended_regimens.summary: Retrieve sperm for cryopreservation and later ICSI.

alternative_regimens.name: proximal vas deferens sperm aspiration
alternative_regimens.summary: A further means of obtaining sperm for later ICSI.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A non-reconstructable inguinal vas deferens defect.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with post-inflammatory or cystic ejaculatory duct obstruction.
decision_rules: Select treatment according to the cause of obstruction.
For obstruction caused by a midline intraprostatic cyst, treat the cyst directly.

recommended_regimens.name: TURED
recommended_regimens.summary: Resect the ejaculatory ducts for post-inflammatory or cystic obstruction.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reported pregnancy rates after TURED are 20-25%.

alternative_regimens.name: incision, unroofing or aspiration of the cyst
alternative_regimens.summary: Treat the causative midline intraprostatic cyst.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Obstruction attributable to a midline intraprostatic cyst.

alternative_regimens.name: seminal vesiculoscopy
alternative_regimens.summary: Remove debris or calculi.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A suitable cause of ejaculatory duct obstruction.

alternative_regimens.name: balloon dilation and laser incision
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative intervention described for calcification identified on TRUS.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Calcification associated with obstruction.

alternative_regimens.name: MESA, PESA, TESA, TESE
alternative_regimens.summary: Obtain sperm for assisted reproduction instead of duct resection.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative to TURED.

alternative_regimens.name: proximal vas deferens sperm aspiration
alternative_regimens.summary: Obtain sperm for assisted reproduction.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative to TURED.

alternative_regimens.name: seminal vesicle-ultrasonically guided aspiration
alternative_regimens.summary: Obtain sperm for assisted reproduction.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative to TURED.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Reported TURED complications include epididymitis, UTI, gross haematuria, haematospermia, azoospermia in partial distal obstruction, and urine reflux into the ejaculatory ducts and seminal vesicles.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with confirmed NOA who are candidates for ART using ICSI.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: Absence of sperm after centrifugation on two consecutive semen analyses
decision_rules: Perform surgical sperm retrieval before ART.
Use microdissection TESE as the preferred retrieval technique, while explaining the low-quality comparative evidence.
Do not use a preliminary diagnostic testicular biopsy or FNA mapping to decide whether to perform definitive retrieval.

recommended_regimens.name: microdissection TESE
recommended_regimens.summary: The guideline panel identifies microdissection TESE as its treatment of choice for sperm retrieval in NOA.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A meta-analysis of case-control studies reported unadjusted sperm retrieval rates of 52% (95% CI: 47-58) for mTESE and 35% (95% CI: 30-40) for TESE; a separate meta-analysis found no difference between the techniques.

alternative_regimens.name: conventional TESE
alternative_regimens.summary: An open surgical retrieval approach discussed in the evidence review.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A surgical alternative, although the panel favours mTESE because available data suggest fewer complications.

not_recommended.name: FNA
not_recommended.reason: Retrieval rates are lower than with TESE and a separate therapeutic operation may be required.

not_recommended.name: TESA
not_recommended.reason: Retrieval rates are lower than with TESE.

not_recommended.name: FNA mapping before definitive TESE
not_recommended.reason: It requires a subsequent invasive therapeutic procedure, may increase testicular damage and lacks adequate cost-benefit justification.

not_recommended.name: testicular biopsy before TESE
not_recommended.reason: A separate diagnostic biopsy is not recommended before therapeutic retrieval.

supportive_care: Provide genetic counselling before ART when genetic abnormalities are identified.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No definitive preoperative predictor of sperm retrieval has been established. The panel’s preference for mTESE is based on low-quality evidence; larger RCTs are needed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with NOA after unsuccessful prior cTESE, TESA or mTESE.
decision_rules: Consider the reported possibility of sperm retrieval at salvage mTESE without treating retrospective findings as a guaranteed benefit.

alternative_regimens.name: salvage mTESE
alternative_regimens.summary: A further surgical attempt after unsuccessful sperm retrieval.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Previously failed cTESE, TESA or mTESE, following individual counselling.

response_assessment.interpretation: One study reported sperm retrieval in 46.5% after failed cTESE or TESA; reports after failed mTESE ranged from 18.4% to 42.8%.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The suggested predictive value of hypospermatogenesis after failed cTESE is based on small retrospective studies.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with NOA being considered for hormonal stimulation before c/mTESE.
decision_rules: Do not start hormonal stimulation before TESE outside clinical trials.
In NOA with hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, do not use preoperative medical therapy routinely to improve sperm recovery.

not_recommended.name: hormonal stimulation before TESE outside clinical trials
not_recommended.reason: Evidence of improved retrieval in NOA is limited, and no RCT has shown a benefit in idiopathic NOA.

not_recommended.name: routine medical therapy before c/mTESE in NOA with hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism
not_recommended.reason: Conclusive evidence of improved sperm recovery is unavailable.

supportive_care: Counsel patients about the limited evidence for hormonal stimulation before retrieval surgery.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A meta-analysis suggested possible benefit in eugonadal but not hypergonadotropic hypogonadal patients; the included studies had moderate or severe risk of bias.

special_populations.population: Couples with advanced maternal age or limited ovarian reserve
special_populations.considerations: The female partner’s age and ovarian reserve can affect when and how the male partner is investigated and treated. Whether to begin evaluation after 6 months without conception when the female partner is older than 35 years remains debated.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider the female partner’s ovarian reserve when choosing the timing of ART rather than surgical intervention.

special_populations.considerations: Advanced paternal age is identified as a risk factor for male factor infertility. SDF was higher in older age groups in a cohort study of 10,000 semen samples.
Most adolescents with varicocele will not have fertility problems later, so prophylactic intervention carries a substantial risk of overtreatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer surgery when a persistently smaller testis has a size difference of > 2 mL or 20%, confirmed at two subsequent visits six months apart.

special_populations.considerations: Management depends on whether the condition is unilateral or bilateral and on contralateral testicular function. Undescended testes carry a risk of GCNIS and GCT.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use hormonal treatment after puberty. Offer orchidectomy for unilateral undescended testis when hormonal function and spermatogenesis are normal. If biochemical hypogonadism or spermatogenic failure is present, offer unilateral or bilateral orchidopexy when technically feasible; obtain simultaneous testicular biopsies when correcting undescended testes in adulthood.

special_populations.population: Men with a history of cryptorchidism
special_populations.considerations: A history of cryptorchidism is associated with impaired semen parameters, possible later hypogonadism and increased testicular cancer risk. Men with unilateral disease may also have abnormalities in the contralateral descended testis.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Counsel about testicular cancer risk and regular testicular self-examination, and screen for hypogonadism.

special_populations.population: Pre-pubertal or peri-pubertal boys with Klinefelter syndrome
special_populations.considerations: Retrieval and cryopreservation of testicular spermatogonial stem cells remain experimental. The same restriction applies to sperm retrieval in older boys who have not considered their fertility potential.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Perform these retrieval procedures only in a research setting.

special_populations.population: Men with Klinefelter syndrome seeking fertility treatment
special_populations.considerations: Sperm production varies, particularly with mosaicism. In azoospermic patients, sperm can be recovered in up to 50% of cases. These men also require follow-up for endocrine and broader health problems.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: TESE or mTESE may be used for sperm retrieval in azoospermic patients. Consider testosterone therapy for hypogonadal testosterone levels after fertility issues have been addressed.

special_populations.population: Men with TGCT or other cancer before gonadotoxic treatment
special_populations.considerations: Semen quality may already be impaired at TGCT diagnosis, and cancer treatment or ablative surgery can further compromise reproduction. Fertility preservation should be discussed before treatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer sperm cryopreservation before planned orchidectomy or other gonadotoxic oncological treatment. Offer onco-TESE during radical orchidectomy to men with testicular cancer and azoospermia or severe semen abnormalities. Do not unduly delay orchidectomy if cryopreservation is unavailable or would delay treatment.

special_populations.population: Men receiving chemotherapy or RT for TGCT
special_populations.considerations: These treatments are teratogenic and can impair fertility. The document reports that sperm aneuploidy may remain increased for up to two years after gonadotoxic therapy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use contraception during treatment and for at least six months after completion.

special_populations.considerations: Survivors have increased risks of hypogonadism, sexual dysfunction and CVD. The risk of hypogonadism is greatest at 6-12 months after treatment, and Leydig cell function may subsequently improve.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Provide multidisciplinary late-effects and survivorship care and assess serum testosterone. It is reasonable to defer testosterone therapy until signs or symptoms of deficiency persist; in men prioritising fertility, balance its use against potential worsening of spermatogenesis.

special_populations.considerations: Additional factors, including bilateral TM, testicular atrophy, undescended testes or a history of TGCT, affect concern about GCNIS. Most men with asymptomatic TM do not develop testicular cancer.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Advise self-examination. Do not perform biopsy, follow-up scrotal US, biochemical tumour markers, or abdominal or pelvic computed tomography for isolated TM without associated risk factors. Offer biopsy to infertile men with TM in the specified higher-risk groups.

special_populations.population: Men with CBAVD or structural absence of the vas deferens and their partners
special_populations.considerations: CFTR mutations may be involved. If the female partner carries a CFTR mutation, the stated risk of a child with CF or CBAVD is 50%, depending on the parental mutations.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Test eligible men and their partners for CFTR mutations and provide genetic counselling before deciding whether to proceed with ICSI. Sperm aspiration or extraction with ICSI can be used in patients with CBAVD.
conditions: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD)

special_populations.population: Men with Y-chromosome microdeletions seeking ICSI
special_populations.considerations: Male offspring will inherit the deletion. Complete deletions involving AZFa and AZFb have a very poor prognosis for surgical sperm retrieval.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Counsel the couple about transmission to sons. Do not perform TESE when complete deletions include AZFa and AZFb.

special_populations.population: Men with high SDF after recurrent pregnancy loss or unsuccessful ART
special_populations.considerations: Use of testicular rather than ejaculated sperm may improve outcomes, but the evidence is limited and large randomised studies have not confirmed the advantage.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Testicular sperm for ICSI may be considered experimental on a case-by-case basis after discussion with reproductive specialists. First address common associations of raised SDF and consider contributing female factors.

special_populations.population: Men with post-pubertal secondary hypogonadism who wish to conceive

special_populations.considerations: The female partner’s ovarian reserve affects the choice between reconstructive surgery and direct ICSI.

document_sections.heading: 11. MALE INFERTILITY
document_sections.content: This chapter addresses the definition, causes, assessment and management of male infertility.

document_sections.heading: 11.1 Definition and classification
document_sections.content: Infertility means that a sexually active couple using no contraception has not conceived spontaneously within 12 months. Primary infertility applies when a couple has never had a child and has not conceived after at least 12 consecutive months of intercourse without contraception; secondary infertility applies when a couple has conceived previously, whether with the same or another partner. In 30-40% of cases, impaired sperm parameters have no identified male-associated explanation; this has historically been called idiopathic male infertility. Such men lack a history, examination findings or endocrine, genetic or biochemical test abnormalities explaining infertility, although semen findings may be abnormal. Possible previously unrecognised contributors include pollution-related endocrine disruption, reactive oxygen species (ROS)/sperm DNA damage, and genetic or epigenetic abnormalities. Unexplained male infertility denotes infertility of unknown origin despite normal sperm parameters and partner assessment; it affects between 20 and 30% of couples.

document_sections.heading: 11.2 Epidemiology/aetiology/pathophysiology/risk factors
document_sections.content: About 15% of couples seek infertility care after failing to conceive within 12 consecutive months. Difficulty conceiving a first child affects one in eight couples, and difficulty conceiving another affects one in six. A male-associated factor, usually accompanied by abnormal semen parameters, is identified in 50% of involuntarily childless couples. Every infertile couple should therefore have the male partner assessed by a urologist trained in male reproduction. Potential contributors include congenital or acquired urogenital abnormalities, genetic abnormalities, malignancy, urogenital infection, varicocele, raised scrotal temperature, endocrine or immunological factors, prior scrotal surgery and exposure to gonadotoxic radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Advanced paternal age is an additional risk factor. The female partner’s age and ovarian reserve may affect the choice and timing of assisted reproductive technology (ART) or surgery. Assessment after 6 months without conception when the female partner is older than 35 years remains debated. Table 11.1 reports the distribution of male infertility causes and associated factors across its stated patient groups.

document_sections.heading: 11.2.2 Summary of evidence and recommendations on epidemiology and aetiology of male infertility
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that infertility affects 15% of reproductive-age couples (LE 3); an identifiable male factor occurs in about 50% (LE 2a), and an isolated male factor in about 20% (LE 2a). Genetic and urogenital abnormalities, endocrine disease, malignancy and gonadotoxic treatment are possible causes (LE 2a). Strong recommendations call for infertility assessment after twelve consecutive months of regular unprotected intercourse, simultaneous investigation of both partners, and assessment of every man in a couple seeking fertility care.

document_sections.heading: 11.3 Diagnostic work-up
document_sections.content: Semen findings inform treatment and are commonly used as a surrogate for male fertility, but semen analysis alone cannot separate fertile from infertile men. The panel considers comprehensive andrological examination necessary regardless of whether semen parameters meet reference values. Infertile men should receive counselling and follow-up because of increased subsequent malignant and non-malignant comorbidity. Core assessment comprises medical and reproductive history, physical examination, semen analysis using World Health Organization (WHO) references, and hormonal evaluation. Clinical features and semen findings may justify genetic testing or imaging.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.1 Medical/reproductive history and physical examination
document_sections.content: The medical history should identify behavioural and lifestyle risks, family history including testicular cancer, systemic and other comorbidities, genitourinary or sexually transmitted infection, prior testicular surgery, gonadotoxic medication and recreational drug use. Pertinent histories include unilateral or bilateral cryptorchidism, torsion, trauma, environmental toxins, anabolic drugs, chemotherapy, radiation and cytotoxic agents. Every infertile man requires a focused examination of secondary sexual characteristics; testicular size, texture and consistency; the vasa deferentia and epididymides; varicocele; palpable genital abnormalities; penile abnormalities; body-hair pattern; and gynaecomastia. Prader’s orchidometer is used clinically to estimate volume but may overestimate ultrasound measurements, and its population-dependent reference values are not uniform. Mean orchidometer-derived testicular volume is 20.0 ± 5.0 mL in the European general population and 18.0 ± 5.0 mL in infertile patients. Abnormal secondary sexual characteristics, testes or testicular volume, masses, absent testes, gynaecomastia and varicocele may suggest testicular deficiency.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.2 Semen analysis
document_sections.content: The 6th edition of the WHO semen manual, published in July 2021, addresses semen examination, sperm preparation and cryopreservation, and quality assurance. Examinations are designated basic, extended or advanced. Laboratories should quantify sperm even below 2 million/mL, acknowledging greater counting error at low counts; total sperm number per ejaculate is more diagnostically useful than concentration, making accurate volume measurement important. Motility categories are fast progressive, slow progressive, non-progressive and immotile (grade a, b, c or d). Morphology assessment uses Tygerberg strict criteria with sperm-adapted Papanicolaou staining; vitality is indicated only when more than 60% of spermatozoa are immotile. Extended procedures assess inflammation, sperm antibodies and defects, ejaculation sequence, aneuploidy, biochemistry and sperm DNA fragmentation (SDF). Table 11.2 gives lower fifth-centile semen references and other consensus thresholds. These references derive from approximately 3,500 men in 12 countries who conceived naturally within 12 months and do not distinguish fertility from infertility; prediction of live birth requires assessment of both partners’ reproductive potential. More complex testing may be useful after recurrent pregnancy loss or with unexplained male infertility. Increased sperm DNA damage is associated with pregnancy failure, although heterogeneous studies preclude definitive conclusions. One semen analysis suffices if WHO results are normal; abnormal findings on at least two tests warrant further andrological investigation. No single sperm parameter establishes infertility. WHO 5th edition categories include oligozoospermia, < 16 million sperm/mL; asthenozoospermia, < 32% progressively motile sperm; and teratozoospermia, < 4% normal forms. The WHO 6th edition does not report this subdivision, but the panel finds it clinically useful. Combined abnormalities constitute oligo-astheno-terato-zoospermia (OAT) syndrome. Azoospermia is complete absence of sperm in semen; severe oligozoospermia, spermatozoa < 5 million/mL, and azoospermia are associated with more obstruction and genetic abnormalities. Azoospermia requires investigation to distinguish obstructive from non-obstructive disease. Centrifugation at 3,000 g for 15 minutes followed by phase-contrast inspection of the pellet at ×200 magnification, with staining and repeat microscopy if needed, helps distinguish absolute azoospermia from cryptozoospermia and identify sperm potentially usable for intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI).

document_sections.heading: Advanced examinations
document_sections.content: Human-oocyte and zona-pellucida binding and hamster-oocyte penetration tests have been removed as obsolete. Research examinations address ROS, oxidative stress, ion channels, acrosome reaction, sperm chromatin and computerassisted sperm analysis (CASA).

document_sections.heading: Measurement of Oxidative Stress
document_sections.content: Oxidative stress can impair sperm quality, function and DNA integrity; associated outcomes include poorer embryonic development, miscarriage and infertility. Sperm have limited capacity to repair DNA damage. Smoking and environmental exposures are associated with oxidative stress. Antioxidants and lifestyle measures might reduce DNA fragmentation and improve sperm quality, but RCTs have not supported these data. Although ROS can be assayed, no standardised ROS test exists; routine measurement should remain experimental pending RCT validation.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.3 Measurement of sperm DNA Fragmentation Index (SDF)
document_sections.content: Sperm DNA fragmentation comprises single- and double-strand breaks; increased fragmentation has been linked to reduced natural conception, infertility and poorer ART outcomes, including impaired embryo development, miscarriage, recurrent pregnancy loss and birth defects. No study has unequivocally and directly established how SDF testing changes infertile-couple management. Hormonal abnormalities, varicocele, chronic infection, smoking and older age may increase fragmentation. Repeated ejaculation 3 hours apart reportedly significantly reduced SDF; an analysis of 10,000 samples found higher SDF in older age groups. Whether available assays reliably predict ART outcomes or should be used routinely is disputed. TUNEL and alkaline COMET assess DNA damage directly; SCSA and SCD assess fragmentation indirectly. SCSA reports the DNA fragmentation index (DFI) and high DNA stainability. An SCSA DFI threshold of 25% has been suggested to correlate with lower natural-conception or intra-uterine insemination (IUI) pregnancy rates, while DFI > 50% correlates with poorer in vitro fertilisation (IVF) outcomes. COMET-derived measures may aid infertility diagnosis and prediction of IVF and ICSI live births. A meta-analysis involving seven SCSA, nine SCD and eight TUNEL studies associated SDF with recurrent pregnancy loss, but was limited by small individual trials and heterogeneous definitions and inclusion criteria. Testicular sperm reportedly have less fragmentation than ejaculated sperm and might improve ICSI outcomes in men with high ejaculated SDF. TESE may be considered after failed ART in unexplained infertility with high fragmentation, with counselling that live-birth reporting is limited and the procedure is invasive. Benefits in cryptozoospermia or oligozoospermia remain unconfirmed by large randomised studies; a suggestive TESE-ICSI meta-analysis was substantially heterogeneous and called for RCTs. Case-by-case use of testicular sperm should follow discussion with reproductive specialists, counselling about weak evidence, evaluation of female factors, and attention to varicocele, diet and lifestyle, accessory gland infection and abstinence duration.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.4 Hormonal determinations
document_sections.content: Testicular deficiency usually produces hypergonadotropic or primary hypogonadism, with raised FSH and LH and testosterone that may be low. FSH generally correlates inversely with spermatogonial numbers: it is usually high when spermatogonia are absent or markedly reduced, but can remain normal with later maturation arrest. Neither FSH nor normal testicular volume reliably excludes sperm retrieval with TESE; men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) and high FSH may have focal spermatogenesis. Emerging but unconfirmed findings associate lower preoperative antiMüllerian hormone (AMH) with successful mTESE retrieval.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5 Genetic testing
document_sections.content: Andrology urologists need familiarity with infertility-associated genetic abnormalities for counselling. Routine clinical screening uses peripheral-blood genomic DNA; sperm aneuploidy assessment and preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) are feasible in selected circumstances, such as recurrent miscarriage.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5.1 Chromosomal abnormalities
document_sections.content: Chromosomal abnormalities may affect chromosome number or structure. Pooled data from 11 publications covering 9,766 infertile men found abnormalities in 5.8%, comprising 4.2% sex-chromosome and 1.5% autosomal abnormalities. In three newborn series comprising 94,465 male infants, the corresponding overall incidence was 0.38%; 131 (0.14%) had sex-chromosome and 232 (0.25%) autosomal abnormalities. Abnormalities become more frequent with worsening testicular deficiency. At sperm counts < 5 million/mL, the incidence of predominantly structural autosomal abnormalities was 4%, described as 10-fold higher than in the general population. Men with NOA have the highest risk, particularly of sex-chromosome abnormalities. Karyotyping is currently indicated with azoospermia or spermatozoa < 10 million/mL; the clinical value of this threshold persists pending cost-effectiveness studies that include consequences such as miscarriage and congenital anomalies.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5.1.1 Sex chromosome abnormalities (Klinefelter syndrome and variants [47,XXY; 46,XY/47, XX mosaicism])
document_sections.content: Klinefelter syndrome is the most common sex-chromosome abnormality. Adults often have small, firm testes and primary hypogonadism, although phenotype ranges from normal virilisation to androgen-deficiency features. Infertility and low testicular volume may be the only detectable features; neuropsychological, learning and language difficulties can occur. Leydig-cell impairment and testosterone deficiency are more frequent than in the general population, whereas peri-pubertal deficiency is uncommon. More pronounced hypogonadism and congenital heart or renal abnormalities occur rarely. Germ cells and sperm production vary and are more frequent with 46,XY/47,XXY mosaicism. For azoospermic patients, TESE or mTESE may recover sperm in up to 50% of cases. Some, but not all, evidence favours younger retrieval; no age threshold is available. Medical follow-up is advised because of general health risks. Testosterone therapy may be considered after fertility issues are addressed if levels are hypogonadal. Metabolic and cardiovascular diseases (CVD), venous thromboembolism (VTE), diabetes, particularly when beginning testosterone therapy, and haematological malignancies are increased risks. Retrieval of testicular spermatogonial stem cells in pre- or peri-pubertal boys for cryopreservation remains experimental and should occur only in research; the same applies to retrieval in older boys who have not considered fertility potential.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5.1.2 Autosomal abnormalities
document_sections.content: Offer genetic counselling to couples seeking fertility care, including IVF/ICSI, if the male partner has an autosomal karyotype abnormality. Common examples are Robertsonian and reciprocal translocations, paracentric inversions and marker chromosomes. Structural anomalies can increase fetal aneuploidy or unbalanced chromosomal complements. For IVF/ICSI involving men with translocations, perform PGT or amniocentesis.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5.2 Cystic fibrosis gene mutations
document_sections.content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is autosomal recessive. Among Caucasians, 4% carry mutations in CFTR on chromosome 7p. Its ion-channel protein influences development of the ejaculatory duct, seminal vesicle, vas deferens and distal two-thirds of the epididymis. Approximately 2,000 CFTR mutations have been identified; alterations can cause congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD), whereas CF disease occurs with homozygous mutations. CBAVD occurs in 1% of infertile men and up to 6% of men with obstructive azoospermia. Carefully assess men with azoospermia for absent vasa, especially with semen volume < 1.0 mL and acidic pH < 7.0. MESA, PESA, TESA or TESE with ICSI can achieve pregnancy in CBAVD-only or CF; CBAVD-only is associated with better sperm quality, simpler retrieval and better ICSI outcomes than CF. F508, R117H and W1282X are frequently detected, although mutation frequencies depend on ethnicity. Analyse the 5T allele in each CBAVD patient because it is considered a mild CFTR mutation. Mild CF manifestations, such as previous chest infections, may occur. Test the female partner when the man has CBAVD. If she carries a CFTR mutation, counselling before ICSI should address the 50% risk of a child with CF or CBAVD, dependent on parental mutations. With negative testing for known mutations, her estimated risk of carrying an unknown mutation is ~0.4%.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5.2.1 Unilateral or bilateral absence/abnormality of the vas and renal anomalies
document_sections.content: Congenital unilateral absence of the vas deferens (CUAVD) commonly accompanies absence of the ipsilateral kidney and probably has a different genetic cause. Screen CFTR in men with unilateral vasal absence and normal kidneys. Renal anomalies are rare with CBAVD and CFTR mutations. Undertake abdominal ultrasound for unilateral or bilateral vasal absence without CFTR mutations; findings can include ipsilateral renal absence, pelvic kidney, or bilateral vasal and renal abnormalities.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5.3 Y microdeletions – partial and complete
document_sections.content: Y-chromosome microdeletions involve AZFa, AZFb or AZFc. Partial or complete loss of AZF regions is the most frequent molecular genetic cause of severe oligozoospermia and azoospermia; each region contains genes potentially involved in spermatogenesis.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5.3.1 Clinical implications of Y microdeletions
document_sections.content: Y deletions are not found in normozoospermic men. Their reported frequency is 8-12% in azoospermia and 3-7% in oligozoospermia; at concentrations > 5 million/mL, they are very rare (~0.7%). AZFc accounts for 65-70%, AZFb and AZFb+c or AZFa+b+c for 25-30%, and AZFa for 5%. Complete AZFa deletion correlates with Sertoli cell only syndrome [SCOS]; complete AZFb deletion correlates with spermatogenic arrest. Complete deletions including AZFa and AZFb predict poor TESE retrieval, so TESE should not be attempted. AZFc deletion has a variable phenotype, and testicular sperm are found in 50-75% of affected men. Counsel men with AZFc deletion and oligo-azoospermia or sperm found at TESE that sons will inherit the deletion. Complete AZF deletion does not increase cryptorchidism or testicular cancer risk. A meta-analysis reported a significantly lower ICSI fertilisation rate, but not live-birth or male-birth rates, in men with Y microdeletions versus controls; its studies were limited by sample size. Y-deletion testing has diagnostic and sperm-retrieval prognostic value.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5.3.1.1 Testing for Y microdeletion
