document_sections.content: Traditional AZF testing indications are azoospermia and severe oligozoospermia, with counts < 5 million/mL. A meta-analysis of 37 European and North American studies including n = 12,492 oligo-zoospermic men located most deletions at concentrations ≤ 1 million sperm/mL and < 1% at > 1 million sperm/mL. No universal absolute threshold is established: testing may be offered below < 5 million sperm/mL and must be performed at ≤1 million sperm/mL. European Academy of Andrology (EAA) primers detect > 95% of clinically relevant deletions; its guidance and external quality control have improved testing reliability.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.5.4 Exome sequencing
document_sections.content: Exome sequencing increasingly identifies monogenic causes and candidate or potentially relevant variants in NOA; diagnostic yield in presumed idiopathic spermatogenic failure may rise. Asthenoteratozoospermia case-control series identify variants potentially useful in panels for ciliary and sperm-flagellar phenotypes. Genotyping may improve understanding of severe morphology or functional disorders, but geographically and ethnically diverse validation is required before routine clinical recommendations. MTHFR single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) have been identified as a possible infertility vulnerability in predominantly Asian cohorts. Possible protective oxidative-stress-pathway SNPs remain under study. A meta-analysis suggested a possible infertility-risk role for XRCC1 polymorphism but could not assess gene–environment interaction.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.6 Imaging in infertile men
document_sections.content: Scrotal ultrasound (US) can measure testicular volume, assess architecture and possible dysgenesis or tumours, and identify indirect obstruction signs. Prader’s orchidometer is generally a practical, reliable and economical volume surrogate, but US is useful when hydrocele, testicular position, epididymal enlargement or fibrosis, thick scrotal skin, or a small testis makes orchidometry unreliable. Inhomogeneous US appearance is usually associated with ageing and has also been reported with atrophy or fibrosis. Testicular inhomogeneity alone does not justify diagnostic biopsy.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.6.1 Scrotal US
document_sections.content: Scrotal US is commonly used with oligo-zoospermia or azoospermia and can help diagnose obstruction, neoplasms and varicocele through venous measurements and reflux assessment.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.6.1.1 Testicular neoplasms
document_sections.content: Compared with fertile controls, infertile men had higher testicular cancer risk (pooled OR = 1.91, 95% CI: 1.52-2.42); a study of oligozoospermia reported HR 11.9. A review found ~18fold higher testicular cancer prevalence in infertile men with testicular microcalcification (TM). Routine US screening remains debated because imaging cannot reliably determine whether many lesions are benign. No definitive lesion-size threshold separates benign from malignant masses. A systematic review identified 32 studies and 1692 masses: 28 studies and 1550 masses described scrotal US, and 4 studies and 142 masses described MRI. In post-pubertal men, masses ≤0.5 cm had significantly lower malignancy odds than masses > 0.5 cm (p < 0.001); masses 0.6-1.0 cm also had lower odds than masses > 1.5 cm (p = 0.04). The comparison of 0.6-1.0 with 1.1-1.5 cm was not significant. Lower malignancy odds were reported for heterogeneous versus homogeneous masses (p = 0.04), hyperechogenic versus hypoechogenic masses (p < 0.01), normal versus increased enhancement (p < 0.01), and peripheral versus central vascularity (p < 0.01). Data were limited for pre-pubertal US and MRI and post-pubertal MRI. Small echogenic areas can reflect benign abnormalities; periodic US assessment is warranted, particularly with malignancy risk factors. Lesion growth or added risks may prompt consideration of biopsy or surgery, although evidence is limited. In a series of 145 men with azoospermia, 49 (34%) had focal US findings, including 20 (14%) hypoechoic lesions, 10 (7%) hyperechoic lesions and 19 (13%) heterogeneous testes. Among 18 evaluable patients, 11 lesions measured < 5 mm and all were benign; other sampled hyperechoic or heterogeneous findings were also benign. Those authors suggested surveillance for severe infertility with negative tumour markers and lesions < 5 mm, with biopsy considered for larger or growing findings. Other studies suggested surveillance might replace radical surgery for avascular hyperechoic lesions with negative markers; hypoechoic vascular lesions are more likely malignant. Because most lesions remain indeterminate on US, histology and multidisciplinary discussion, including invasive diagnostic options, should be considered. US-guided biopsy with intra-operative frozen section can be offered as an alternative to radical orchidectomy after counselling and multidisciplinary review; concurrent TESE and sperm banking are possible in azoospermia.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.6.1.2 Varicocele
document_sections.content: Varicocele decisions principally rely on examination. Colour Doppler US can assess reflux and venous diameter when palpation is unreliable and can identify postoperative persistence or recurrence; these measurements may inform treatment decisions.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.6.1.3 Other
document_sections.content: Scrotal US can identify proximal seminal-tract obstruction. In CBAVD, described epididymal appearances include tubular ectasia with a honeycomb pattern, a meshwork pattern, and partial or complete epididymal absence.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.6.2 Transrectal US
document_sections.content: When low semen volume, acidic pH and severe oligozoospermia or azoospermia suggest obstruction, scrotal and transrectal US can assess CBAVD and epididymal or seminal-vesicle abnormalities. Transrectal US (TRUS) also evaluates obstructive azoospermia from CBAVD or ejaculatory-duct abnormalities, including cysts and seminal-vesicle dilatation, hypoplasia or atrophy. Retrograde ejaculation should be excluded as a differential diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: 11.3.7 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic work-up of male infertility
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that semen analysis alone cannot establish fertility (LE 2a); male infertility predicts malignant and non-malignant comorbidity (LE 2a); core history, examination, semen and hormonal assessment are important (LE 2a); genetic testing and imaging may depend on presentation (LE 2a); and orchidometry or US can measure testicular volume (LE 2a). WHO semen references use the lower 5th percentiles from 3,500 men who conceived within 12 consecutive months (LE 3). Oxidative stress harms sperm, but validated ROS assays are lacking (LE 2b). High SDF is associated with lower natural or IUI pregnancy rates, adverse ART outcomes, recurrent pregnancy loss and unexplained infertility (LE 2a); a possible testicular-sperm advantage for ICSI remains unconfirmed in large RCTs (LE 3). Gonadotropins and total testosterone help classify hypogonadism (LE 2a), and FSH is negatively associated with sperm count (LE 2a). The summary also covers chromosomal abnormalities, Klinefelter syndrome, CFTR and CBAVD, renal anomalies, Y microdeletions and inherited risk, emerging exome-sequencing yield, US findings, cancer risk and multidisciplinary assessment of indeterminate lesions (principally LE 2a); transrectal US for suspected distal obstruction is assigned LE 2b. Strong recommendations are to assess the female partner’s fertility and ovarian reserve in parallel; examine men seeking help; obtain comprehensive history, risk assessment, examination and semen analysis; follow the latest WHO semen manual; repeat an abnormal baseline semen test with at least two consecutive analyses; test SDF after recurrent natural-conception loss, ART failure or unexplained infertility; obtain testosterone and Follicle Stimulating Hormone/Luteinising Hormone at least in oligozoospermia or azoospermia; offer karyotyping and counselling in azoospermia or spermatozoa < 5 million/mL; follow men with Klinefelter syndrome endocrinologically; test Y microdeletions at ≤ 1 million sperm/mL and consider testing at < 5 million sperm/mL; counsel about transmission to sons; avoid extraction with complete deletions involving AZFa and AZFb; test indicated men and partners for CFTR; counsel couples with relevant genetic findings; and perform transrectal US for suspected partial or complete distal obstruction. Weak recommendations address counselling on health risks, measuring testicular volume by orchidometry or US, not using ROS tests routinely, treating testicular sperm for high ejaculated SDF as experimental, performing scrotal US because of testicular cancer risk, and discussing invasive options for indeterminate lesions in a multidisciplinary setting.

document_sections.heading: 11.4 Special Conditions and Relevant Clinical Entities
document_sections.content: This part addresses specific conditions associated with male infertility.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1 Cryptorchidism
document_sections.content: Cryptorchidism is the most common congenital male genital abnormality. At 1 year, nearly 1% of full-term boys are affected; approximately 30% of undescended testes cannot be palpated and may be intra-abdominal. This guideline’s management discussion concerns adults.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1.1 Classification
document_sections.content: Classification considers duration, laterality and anatomical location. Congenital cases are present from birth; acquired cases occur after the testis had been scrotal. Sites include inguinal, intra-abdominal and ectopic. Studies found similar subsequent hormone profiles, semen results and volumes after treatment of congenital or acquired cases. Adults treated for congenital bilateral disease have lower volume and hormonal function than those treated for unilateral disease.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1.1.1 Aetiology and pathophysiology
document_sections.content: Cryptorchidism has been proposed as part of testicular dysgenesis syndrome (TDS), potentially involving early-pregnancy environmental or genetic influences, including endocrine disruptors. TDS also encompasses hypospadias, impaired fertility, malignancy risk and Leydig/Sertoli-cell dysfunction. Maternal gestational smoking and prematurity have also been linked to cryptorchidism.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1.1.2 Pathophysiological effects in maldescended testes
document_sections.content: Undescended testes can undergo germ-cell degeneration and have subsequent fertility and cancer implications.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1.1.2.1 Degeneration of germ cells
document_sections.content: Germ-cell degeneration is evident after the first year and differs by testicular position; cell numbers decline further during the second year. Treatment between six to 18 months is recommended to preserve future spermatogenesis and hormone production and reduce tumour risk. Surgery is most effective. Meta-analyses report poor descent rates with GnRH or hCG, and hCG might harm later spermatogenesis. The cited paediatric EAU guidance does not recommend routine endocrine treatment for descent but recommends GnRH analogues for bilateral undescended testes in boys. Evidence also suggests a normally descended contralateral testis in unilateral disease can have reduced size, altered consistency and lower future-fertility markers; counsel patients and parents accordingly.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1.1.2.2 Relationship with fertility
document_sections.content: Semen parameters are often impaired after cryptorchidism, and earlier surgery may improve later fertility. Paternity after unilateral cryptorchidism is reported as 89.7%, versus 93.7% without cryptorchidism. In untreated bilateral disease, 100% were oligospermic and 75% azoospermic; after successful bilateral treatment, 75% remained oligospermic and 42% azoospermic. Screen for hypogonadism as a possible long-term consequence relevant to fertility, testosterone deficiency and MetS.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1.1.2.3 Germ cell tumours
document_sections.content: Cryptorchidism increases risk of testicular microcalcification, intratubular germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) and testicular cancer. A cryptorchidism history occurs in 5-10% of testicular cancers. Germ-cell-tumour risk is 3.6-7.4 times the general-population risk, and 2-6% of men with a history of cryptorchidism develop a testicular tumour. Prepubertal orchidopexy reportedly reduces cancer risk, but risk remains above that of men without cryptorchidism. Counsel all affected men about increased risk and regular self-examination.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1.2.1 Hormonal treatment
document_sections.content: Human chorionic gonadotropin and GnRH are not recommended to treat cryptorchidism in adults.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1.2.2 Surgical treatment
document_sections.content: Removal of an intra-abdominal testis in adolescence can be recommended when the other testis is normal because of malignancy risk. Adults with a palpable undescended testis and a normally functioning contralateral testis may be offered orchidectomy because of GCNIS and future germ-cell-tumour risk and the inability to self-examine that testis. With unilateral undescended testis and contralateral biochemical hypogonadism or impaired sperm production, orchidopexy may preserve hormones and fertility; panel consensus recommends multiple biopsies during orchidopexy to assess GCNIS. Bilateral correction even in adulthood may permit sperm production in previously azoospermic men and can be considered when fertility preservation is valued. Vascular injury is the most severe orchidopexy complication; atrophy occurs in 1-2% of cases, was 12% in non-palpable testes with long vascular pedicles permitting scrotal positioning, and has been reported in up to 40% after staged orchidopexy. During orchidectomy for germ-cell tumour, offer contralateral biopsy to patients at high GCNIS risk, including cryptorchidism history, testicular volume < 12 mL or poor spermatogenesis.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.1.3 Summary of evidence recommendations for cryptorchidism
document_sections.content: Evidence identifies multifactorial genetic and endocrine-disruption origins (LE 2a), an association with testicular dysgenesis, infertility and germ-cell tumours requiring counselling (LE 2b), near-equivalent paternity after corrected unilateral disease (LE 1b), and significantly poorer paternity prospects with bilateral disease (LE 1b). Strong recommendations prohibit hormonal treatment after puberty, require simultaneous biopsy to assess GCNIS during adult correction, and offer orchidectomy to adults with unilateral undescended testis and normal hormone function and spermatogenesis. Offering technically feasible unilateral or bilateral orchidopexy with biochemical hypogonadism or spermatogenic failure is Weak.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.2 Germ cell malignancy and male infertility
document_sections.content: Testicular germ cell tumour (TGCT) is the most common cancer in Caucasian men aged 15-40 years and affects approximately 1% of sub-fertile men. Annual incidence in Caucasians ranges from 10/100,000 in Denmark and Norway to 2/100,000 in Finland and the Baltic countries. Seminomas and nonseminomas are usually preceded by GCNIS, which may progress to invasive cancer untreated. Cancer incidence has increased in countries with reliable registries, alongside deteriorating male reproductive health in western countries. A possible connection to TDS and pregnancy-related genetic or environmental influences has been proposed. Endocrine-disrupting chemicals have also been associated with sexual dysfunction and abnormal semen. Ultrasound-visible microcalcification may accompany TGCT or GCNIS.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.2.1 Testicular germ cell cancer and reproductive function
document_sections.content: Offer all men with cancer sperm cryopreservation before gonadotoxic treatment or surgery that may impair sperm production or ejaculation. Before TGCT treatment, azoospermia has been observed in 24% and oligospermia in 50%. With average 10-year testicular-cancer survival of 98%, counsel about fertility preservation before treatment. Offer ejaculated-sperm preservation as the most cost-effective approach or surgically retrieved sperm when appropriate. In azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia, cryopreservation before orchidectomy permits consideration of concurrent TESE. Networks enabling referral for TESE are recommended. Underuse of semen assessment and banking can miss candidates for oncoTESE. Contemporary practice does not support the claim that pre-orchidectomy cryopreservation necessarily delays treatment; its survival impact has not been investigated. Do not unduly delay orchidectomy when cryopreservation is unavailable or would delay care. Because chemotherapy and radiotherapy (RT) are teratogenic, use contraception throughout treatment and for at least six months afterward. Long-term infertility after RT is rare; chemotherapy effects depend on cumulative dose. TGCT treatment may reduce semen quality, increase sperm aneuploidy up to two years, and increase DNA damage and SDF. Spermatogenesis usually recovers one to four years after chemotherapy; aneuploidy often approaches pretreatment levels at 18-24 months. Studies of survivors’ offspring have not demonstrated a significant increase in genetic abnormalities after prior chemotherapy or radiotherapy. TGCT can impair Leydig cells even contralaterally. Pretreatment testosterone, SHBG, LH and oestradiol may establish hypogonadism risk and baseline. Survivors’ testosterone should be assessed; hypogonadism risk is greatest at 6-12 months and may subsequently improve, so testosterone treatment may reasonably await persistent symptoms or signs. Sexual dysfunction and CVD risks are also increased. Multidisciplinary survivorship care may address psychological, medical and social needs. When fertility matters, weigh testosterone’s effect on spermatogenesis; selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs; e.g., clomiphene) or gonadotrophin analogues (e.g., hCG) may be considered off-label.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.2.2 Testicular microcalcification (TM)
document_sections.content: TM occurs in 0.6-9% of men referred for testicular US; its general-population incidence is unknown and probably low. It has been observed with malignancy and several benign reproductive conditions, and reported TGCT-associated incidence is 6-46%. Its association with infertility is uncertain. A case-control meta-analysis associated TM in infertile men with testicular cancer (pooled OR: 18.11, 95% CI: 8.09, 40.55; p < 0.0001). Although TM merits counselling in this setting and biopsies show more GCNIS, especially with bilateral findings, calcification itself is not malignant and its association with TGCT remains controversial. Possible GCNIS risk factors include infertility, atrophy, undescended testis, prior TGCT and contralateral TM; biopsy has been suggested for selected patients after discussion of its risks. Most asymptomatic patients do not develop cancer. Decastro et al. suggested no testicular cancer developed in most men with TM (98.4%) during 5-year follow-up; extensive screening would therefore principally benefit high-risk men. Advise regular self-examination with incidental TM, particularly with other cancer risks. Annual urological examination and US have been suggested for higher-risk men, but follow-up may be difficult; evidence is lacking for higher cancer prevalence specifically with both TM and atrophy.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.2.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for germ cell malignancy and testicular microcalcification
document_sections.content: The evidence summary reports TGCT in approximately 1% of sub-fertile men (LE 2b); frequent abnormal semen at diagnosis (LE 2a); potential identification of oncoTESE candidates through semen testing and cryopreservation before orchidectomy (LE 2b); treatment-associated reproductive, endocrine, sexual and cardiovascular effects (LE 2a); TM in benign and malignant settings (LE 2a); higher cancer risk with TM in infertile men (LE 1a); higher-risk GCNIS groups (LE 2a); and lack of indication for extensive screening or invasive biopsy for isolated TM (LE 2b). Advising self-examination even for TM without added risk is Weak. Do not perform biopsy, surveillance US, biochemical tumour markers, or abdominal or pelvic computed tomography for isolated TM without additional risks (Strong). Offer biopsy to infertile men with TM in specified higher-risk groups, including atrophic testes < 12 mL (Weak). For suspicious findings with TM-associated lesions, undertake inguinal exploration and biopsy or offer orchidectomy after multidisciplinary and patient discussion (Strong). Multidisciplinary late-effects and survivorship care after TGCT, cryopreservation before planned orchidectomy or further oncological treatment, and onco-TESE during radical orchidectomy when azoospermia or severe semen abnormalities are present are Strong recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.3 Varicocele
document_sections.content: Varicocele may accompany impaired ipsilateral testicular development, subfertility, pain or discomfort, and hypogonadism.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.3.1 Classification
document_sections.content: Subclinical varicocele is not palpable or visible at rest or with Valsalva but is detectable by special testing. Grade 1 is palpable with Valsalva; Grade 2 is palpable at rest; Grade 3 is visible and palpable at rest.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.3.2 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Physical examination establishes the diagnosis. Scrotal Doppler US is indicated when examination is inconclusive or semen remains unsatisfactory after repair, to assess persistence or recurrence. Upright Valsalva venous diameter > 3 mm and reflux lasting > 2 seconds correlate with clinically significant disease. Testicular volume should use Lambert’s formula (V=L x W x H x 0.71). Investigate an isolated clinical right-sided varicocele further for abdominal, retroperitoneal or congenital abnormalities.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.3.3.1 Varicocele and fertility
document_sections.content: Varicocele occurs in almost 15% of the general male population, 25% of men with abnormal semen and 35-40% of men presenting with infertility. Estimated incidence is 35–44% in primary infertility and 45–81% in secondary infertility. Higher grade and age are associated with worsening semen findings. The precise fertility relationship is uncertain; raised scrotal temperature, hypoxia and reflux of toxic metabolites may contribute to testicular dysfunction and DNA damage.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.3.3.2 Varicocelectomy
document_sections.content: Reviews of clinical varicocele suggest repair improves semen parameters in selected men with abnormalities, including some with NOA; postoperative pain resolves in 48-90%. Greater benefit has been reported with higher-grade disease. Randomised evidence found subclinical-varicocele treatment ineffective for increasing spontaneous pregnancy, and studies mainly involving normal semen did not favour treatment over observation. In abnormal-semen groups, one review reported improved pregnancy (OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.00–1.65, p = 0.04) and total sperm count (mean difference: 12.34 million/ml, 95% CI 3.49–21.18, p = 0.006) versus observation, without demonstrated between-group benefit for progressive motility or normal morphology. Within treated participants, before–after comparisons favoured count, motility and morphology. Another review compared n=1,426 repaired men with n=996 untreated controls and reported postoperative differences in concentration (SMD 1.73; 95% CI 1.12 to 2.34; p<0.001), total count (SMD 1.89; 95% CI 0.56 to 3.22; p < 0.05), progressive motility (SMD 3.30; 95% CI 2.16 to 4.43; p < 0.01), total motility (SMD 0.88; 95% CI 0.03 to 1.73; p=0.04) and normal morphology (SMD 1.67; 95% CI 0.87 to 2.47; p < 0.05). A 2012 Cochrane review suggested improved spontaneous conception in otherwise unexplained subfertility; a 2021 review of 5,384 participants found pregnancy may improve versus delayed or no treatment (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.26). Two RCT meta-analyses favoured treatment in clinical varicocele with oligozoospermia and otherwise unexplained infertility, reporting combined OR of 2.39-4.15 (95% CI: 1.56-3.66) and (95% CI: 2.31-7.45), respectively. Semen improvement takes up to two spermatogenic cycles on average; spontaneous pregnancy occurs between 6 and 12 months after surgery. A further meta-analysis suggested better ART outcomes in oligozoospermia (OR of 1.69 [95% CI: 0.95-3.02]).

document_sections.heading: 11.4.3.3.3 Prophylactic varicocelectomy
document_sections.content: Prophylactic adolescent repair risks overtreatment because most affected boys will later conceive without difficulty. It is advised only with serially documented impaired testicular growth and/or abnormal semen.

document_sections.heading: Varicocelectomy and NOA
document_sections.content: Non-randomised studies suggest repair may permit sperm to appear in the ejaculate in NOA. A pooled analysis included 468 patients with NOA and varicocele treated by surgery or embolisation; repaired patients had higher surgical sperm-retrieval rates than unrepaired patients (OR: 2.65; 95% CI: 1.69-4.14; p < 0.001). Postoperative ejaculate contained sperm in 43.9% (range: 20.8%-55.0%), potentially avoiding retrieval surgery. Evidence quality is low; discuss risks and benefits fully and consider underlying genetic defects when interpreting findings.

document_sections.heading: Varicocelectomy and hypogonadism
document_sections.content: Intervention might benefit hypogonadal men with clinical varicocele. A meta-analysis of 712 men found a postoperative versus preoperative mean testosterone increase of 34.3 ng/dL (95% CI: 22.57-46.04, p < 0.00001, I² = 0%) across seven studies; the mean difference versus untreated controls among hypogonadal patients was 105.65 ng/dL (95% CI: 77.99-133.32 ng/dL). Interpret cautiously, compare surgical risks and costs against testosterone treatment, and explain that prospective RCTs are still needed.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.3.3.4 Varicocelectomy for assisted reproductive technology and raised SDF
document_sections.content: Varicocelectomy may improve sperm DNA integrity. A meta-analysis of 1,070 infertile men with clinical varicocele associated surgery with lower postoperative SDF (weighted mean difference 7.23%; 95% CI: 8.86 to 5.59), irrespective of assay or technique. Effects appeared greater at preoperative fragmentation index ≥ 20% than at SDF < 20%; effect size rose with baseline SDF (coefficient: 0.23; 95%CI: 0.07 to 0.39). Following ART failure with high DNA damage, intervention may be considered after extensive counselling and exclusion of other causes. Its role with normal semen remains uncertain; consider ovarian reserve, operative risk and potential ART delay. A retrospective four-study meta-analysis of 870 ICSI cycles compared 438 with previous repair against 432 without and found higher clinical pregnancy (OR 1.59, 95% CI: 1.19-2.12, I2 = 25%) and live birth (OR 2.17, 95% CI: 1.55-3.06, I2 = 0%) after repair. Another ART meta-analysis involving 1,241 patients reported higher live birth in oligospermic men (OR = 1.699) and combined oligo-azoospermic/azoospermic groups (OR = 1.761), higher pregnancy in azoospermic men (OR = 2.336) and the combined groups (OR 1.760), and higher live birth after IUI following intervention (OR 8.360).

document_sections.heading: 11.4.3.4 Disease management
document_sections.content: Table 11.3 compares recurrence, persistence and complications across available varicocele interventions.

document_sections.heading: Impact on pregnancy rate and semen parameters
document_sections.content: Current evidence favours microsurgical varicocelectomy among surgical techniques. A Cochrane review found subinguinal microsurgery probably improves pregnancy slightly more than other operations (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.36). A review subgroup found surgery, but not radiological intervention, significantly improved pregnancy and sperm concentration versus controls. A more recent Cochrane review judged surgery-versus-radiology effects on pregnancy and recurrence inconclusive. Large prospective comparative RCTs are unavailable.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Microsurgery has been associated with fewer complications and recurrences than other techniques but requires specialist training. Other techniques remain options. Radiological sclerotherapy and embolisation are minimally invasive; recurrence comparisons with surgery conflict across analyses. A meta-analysis of twelve studies comparing 738 surgical ligations with 647 sclero-embolisations found no significant overall complication difference (OR 1.48; 95% CI 0.86–2.57, p = 0.16). Hydrocele was significantly more frequent after surgical ligation, whereas postoperative orchiepidydimitys was more frequent with radiological methods. Robot-assisted and microscopic procedures have similar reported success, but larger prospective randomised studies are needed.

document_sections.heading: Table 11.3: Recurrence and complication rates associated with treatments for varicocele
document_sections.content: The table presents recurrence or persistence and reported overall and procedure-specific complications for antegrade or retrograde sclerotherapy, retrograde embolization, open operations, microscopic inguinal or subinguinal repair, and laparoscopy.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for varicocele
document_sections.content: The evidence summary links varicocele to progressive testicular injury and possible reduced fertility (LE 2a); notes adolescent overtreatment risk (LE 3); suggests benefit from repair in selected clinical varicocele with abnormal semen (LE 1a), including improved pregnancy and concentration but less certain motility or morphology benefit (LE 1a); describes low-certainty evidence of sperm appearing after repair in NOA (LE 2); suggests fewer recurrences and complications with microscopic approaches without available RCTs (LE 2a); and associates intervention with reduced SDF and possibly better ART outcomes (LE 2a). Strong recommendations are adolescent surgery for persistent testicular size difference > 2 mL or 20%, verified on two subsequent visits six months apart; no treatment with normal semen or subclinical varicocele; and treatment of infertile men with clinical varicocele, abnormal semen, otherwise unexplained infertility and a partner with good ovarian reserve. Considering varicocelectomy for increased SDF with unexplained infertility or failed ART, including recurrent loss or failed embryogenesis or implantation, is Weak.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4 Male accessory gland infections and infertility
document_sections.content: This section considers male accessory gland infection as a potentially treatable contributor to infertility.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.1 Introduction
document_sections.content: The WHO groups urethritis, prostatitis, orchitis and epididymitis as male accessory gland infections (MAGIs). Evidence about effects of symptomatic or asymptomatic infection on sperm quality conflicts. A review could not establish a strong relationship between sexually transmitted infection and infertility because available studies were limited in quality.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.2.1 Semen analysis
document_sections.content: Semen analysis can provide sperm-quality information and help assess whether the prostate participates in a broader MAGI.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.2.2 Microbiological findings
document_sections.content:
After urinary tract infection, including urethritis, has been excluded, > 106 peroxidase-positive white blood-cells (WBCs) per millilitre of ejaculate indicate inflammation. For suspected genitourinary infection, perform semen culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for common urinary pathogens. Ejaculate concentrations > 103 CFU/mL indicate significant bacteriospermia. Deliver the sample to the laboratory the same day because elapsed time affects organism detection and the strains recovered. The ideal semen test for C. trachomatis is not established, although PCR is the most accurate reported method.

Historical data indicate that Ureaplasma urealyticum is pathogenic only above > 103 CFU/mL ejaculate; fewer than 10% of analysed samples exceeded that concentration. Normal urethral colonisation makes it difficult to interpret mycoplasma findings in ejaculate. A meta-analysis found no association of Ureaplasma parvum or Mycoplasma genitalium with male infertility, but reported relationships for U. urealyticum (OR: 3.03 95% CI: 1.02–8.99) and Mycoplasma hominis (OR: 2.8; 95% CI: 0.93– 3.64). Treatment is therefore not invariably recommended. Human papilloma virus (HPV) has been detected in semen in 20% of infertile populations and 8% of men in the general population. Systematic reviews associated seminal HPV with male infertility and poorer pregnancy outcomes, but prospective validation is needed to establish its clinical impact. Seminal Herpes Simplex virus (HSV)-2 may coincide with poorer sperm quality in infertile men than HSV-negative status; whether antiviral treatment improves fertility is unclear.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.2.3 White blood cells
document_sections.content: The significance of elevated ejaculate leukocytes remains disputed. Leukocytospermia indicates inflammation but does not reliably identify bacterial or viral infection. The WHO threshold is > 106 WBCs/mL, and a seminal peroxidase test should confirm the finding. Two studies in proven prostatitis found higher leukocyte counts than in men without inflammation (CPPS, type NIH 3b). A meta-analysis of case-control studies found that leukocytospermia in men seeking care for couple subfertility was not associated with reduced fertility after ART or poorer semen quality when genital-infection symptoms were absent. Evidence does not show that treating leukocytospermia alone, without identified infectious organisms, improves conception.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.2.4 Sperm quality
document_sections.content: A systematic review of case-controlled studies found adverse effects of chronic prostatitis (CP/CPPS) on sperm density, motility and morphology. C. trachomatis and Ureoplasma spp. can lower sperm density and motility, alter morphology and increase DNA damage. In a retrospective cross-sectional study, U. urealyticum was the most frequent single seminal pathogen among asymptomatic infertile men; positive culture correlated with lower sperm concentration in univariable (p < 0.001) and multivariable (p = 0.04) analyses. Human papilloma virus is associated with altered semen density and sperm motility and DNA damage. Mycoplasma spp. can diminish motility and induce anti-sperm antibodies.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.2.5 Seminal plasma alterations
document_sections.content: Seminal plasma elastase reflects polymorphonuclear lymphocyte activity in ejaculate. Inflammatory cytokines can influence sperm function, although studies found no correlation between interleukin concentrations, leukocytes and sperm function. The prostate is the principal seminal-plasma source of IL-6 and IL-8; IL-6 in particular contributes to accessory-gland inflammation. Raised cytokine concentrations do not depend on leukocyte counts in expressed prostatic secretions.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.2.6 Glandular secretory dysfunction
document_sections.content: Seminal plasma pH, citric acid and γ-glutamine transpeptidase can assess prostatic secretion, although many laboratories no longer measure them. Their concentrations commonly change with infection or inflammation, but they are not recommended as MAGIs diagnostic markers.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.2.7 Reactive oxygen species (ROS)
document_sections.content: ROS may rise in infertile men with asymptomatic seminal C. trachomatis or M. hominis and decline following antibiotics. Because measured ROS levels in these patients are low, firm conclusions are difficult. Chronic urogenital infection also accompanies higher leukocyte counts, whose biological meaning in prostatitis is uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.2.8 Disease management
document_sections.content: Only antibiotic treatment of chronic bacterial prostatitis classified as NIH II has provided symptom relief, microbial eradication and reductions in cellular and humoral inflammatory measures in urogenital secretions. Antibiotics might improve sperm quality, but evidence does not show that treating CP/CPPS increases natural-conception probability. Asymptomatic seminal C. trachomatis or M. hominis may correlate with impaired sperm quality that recovers after antibiotics; confirmation requires further research.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.3 Epididymitis
document_sections.content: Epididymal inflammation generally presents with acutely developing unilateral pain and swelling. Among sexually active men aged < 35 years, C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoea are the usual causes, and sexually transmitted cases generally accompany urethritis. Cases unrelated to sexual transmission are associated with UTIs and occur more often at > 35 years.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.3.1.1 Ejaculate analysis
document_sections.content: Ejaculate assessment using WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (6th edn) criteria can indicate ongoing inflammation. Sperm count and progressive motility may decline transiently, and semen culture may identify pathogens. After bilateral epididymitis, follow-up should particularly consider epididymal-duct stenosis, lower sperm counts and azoospermia.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.3.1.2 Disease management
document_sections.content: Epididymitis treatment seeks microbial cure, relief of clinical findings, prevention of testicular injury and transmission, and fewer complications such as infertility or chronic pain. Patients with confirmed or suspected N. gonorrhoeae- or C. trachomatis-related epididymitis must be told to refer sexual partners for assessment and treatment.

document_sections.heading: 11.4.4.4 Summary of evidence and recommendation for male accessory gland infections
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that a clear association between MAGIs and impaired natural conception has not been established (LE 3). Antibiotics often eradicate organisms without improving inflammatory changes or reversing functional or anatomical deficits (LE 2a). They may improve sperm quality without increasing conception probability (LE 2a). Evidence is insufficient to determine whether antibiotics or antioxidants improve fertility outcomes in infertile men with leukocytospermia (LE 3). The guideline recommends treating MAGIs because sperm quality may improve, while cautioning that conception probability need not improve (Weak). It recommends referral of sexual partners for evaluation and treatment when an accessory sex gland infection is confirmed or suspected to be sexually transmitted (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 11.5 Non-Invasive Male Infertility Management
document_sections.content: This part addresses lifestyle measures, empirical supplements and endocrine treatment for male infertility.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.1.1 Life-style
document_sections.content: Uncontrolled studies suggest that weight loss can improve semen parameters, whereas RCT findings conflict. A meta-analysis of 28 cohort studies involving 1,022 patients found no improvement in sperm quality or function after bariatric surgery in morbid obesity; ART outcome data are unavailable. Weight reduction can improve obesity-associated secondary hypogonadism and might improve outcomes for couples seeking infertility care. A meta-analysis linked moderate-intensity recreational activity (20–40 metabolic equivalents [METs]/week) and high-intensity activity (40–80 METs-h/week) to better semen measures; exercise might also improve the hormonal profile. A meta-analysis of 20 studies involving 5,865 participants associated smoking negatively with sperm parameters. A meta-analysis of 15 cross-sectional studies involving 16,395 men suggested that moderate alcohol use does not harm semen parameters, whereas high intake can impair male fertility. Heavy chronic intake, defined as > 2 drinks/day, can lower testosterone.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.1.2 Antioxidant treatment
document_sections.content: Oxidative stress is considered an important contributor to idiopathic infertility. ROS can impair sperm function through membrane lipid peroxidation, affecting motility, acrosome reaction and chromatin maturation and increasing SDF; seminal ROS has also been negatively associated with ART outcomes. Evidence for antioxidant treatment remains conflicting. A Cochrane review of 34 RCTs and 2,876 couples concluded that antioxidants improved live-birth and pregnancy rates during ART, and a meta-analysis of 61 studies involving 6,264 infertile men aged 18-65 years reported similar findings; the reported study quality was poor. The Males, Antioxidants, and Infertility (MOXI) trial found no improvement over placebo in semen measures or DNA integrity, and cumulative live-birth rates at 6 months did not differ between antioxidants and placebo (15% vs. 24%). The evidence does not establish which antioxidants or treatment schedules would improve semen measures or pregnancy.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.1.3 Probiotic treatment
document_sections.content: Prebiotic/probiotic supplementation might affect hormone release, free-radical removal and the prostatic environment, potentially benefiting sperm function. In an RCT of 56 men with idiopathic infertility, supplementation versus placebo significantly improved sperm concentration, motility, normal morphology and DNA integrity. An RCT involving 78 infertile men after varicocelectomy found a significant early improvement at 3 months in concentration and normal morphology with postoperative probiotics versus placebo. Larger, adequately powered RCTs are needed.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.1.4 Selective oestrogen receptor modulators
document_sections.content: SERMs block hypothalamic oestrogen receptors, increasing GnRH and pituitary gonadotropin release and thereby stimulating spermatogenesis. A meta-analysis of eleven RCTs reported significant improvements in pregnancy, sperm and hormonal outcomes; an updated meta-analysis of sixteen studies reported similar findings. An earlier systematic review did not find an association with pregnancy rates. Few studies were placebo-controlled, overall study quality was low, and complications were insufficiently reported. Consequently, positive findings in idiopathic infertility do not support a conclusive recommendation.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.1.5 Aromatase inhibitors
document_sections.content: Aromatase is a cytochrome p450 enzyme found in testes, prostate, brain, bone and adipose tissue; it converts testosterone and androstenedione into oestradiol and oestrone. Oestradiol suppresses hypothalamic and pituitary gonadotropin secretion, affecting spermatogenesis. AIs may reversibly inhibit aromatase-complex cytochrome p450 isoenzymes 2A6 and 2C19, reducing oestrogen feedback and increasing GnRH pulses and pituitary FSH production. Aromatase activity has been associated with infertility involving testicular dysfunction and low testosterone and/or a low testosterone-to-oestradiol ratio. AIs have been reported to increase endogenous testosterone and improve spermatogenesis as an off-label infertility treatment. Steroidal testolactone and non-steroidal anastrozole and letrozole have significantly improved hormonal and semen measures with a favourable tolerability profile, but prospective RCTs are required to establish efficacy.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.2 Summary of evidence and recommendation for Non-Invasive Male Infertility Management
document_sections.content: The evidence summary links obesity, little physical activity, smoking and high alcohol intake to poorer sperm quality in infertile men (LE 2a). In idiopathic oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia, weight loss, activity, smoking cessation and reduced alcohol might improve sperm quality and conception prospects (LE 2a). Evidence is inconclusive for antioxidants (LE 1b), prebiotic/probiotic supplements (LE 1b), SERMs (LE 1b), and steroidal testolactone or nonsteroidal anastrozole and letrozole (LE 1b) in idiopathic infertility; the first two interventions might nevertheless improve semen parameters. The guideline recommends explaining the effects of obesity, inactivity, smoking and high alcohol consumption on sperm quality and testosterone and advising lifestyle improvement to increase conception chances (Strong). It advises against routine antioxidants, prebiotic/probiotic products, SERMs or AIs for idiopathic infertility (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 11.5.3 Hormonal therapy
document_sections.content: This part distinguishes treatment of secondary hypogonadism, primary hypogonadism, idiopathic male-factor infertility and infertility following anabolic steroid abuse.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.3.1 Secondary hypogonadism
document_sections.content: The guideline refers readers to Appendix 7 for discussion of pre-pubertal-onset disease. For post-pubertal onset, hCG alone is usually used first to initiate spermatogenesis. The suggested starting dose is 250 IU hCG twice weekly; once testosterone normalises, dosing may rise to 2,000 IU twice weekly. Semen should be checked every 3 months unless conception occurs. If spermatogenesis is not stimulated, FSH can be added at 75 IU three times per week, rising to 150 IU three times per week when indicated. FSH and hCG may instead be combined from the outset and can promote better outcomes in HH. A cited comparison found no outcome difference between urinary-derived, highly purified FSH and recombinant FSH. Larger initial testicular volume predicts a better gonadotrophin response. An observation that prior testosterone treatment worsened subsequent outcomes in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism was not confirmed by a later meta-analysis.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.3.1.1 Secondary hypogonadism due to hyperprolactinemia
document_sections.content: When hyperprolactinaemia suppresses gonadotrophins and contributes to sub-fertility, treatment is a dopamine agonist or withdrawal of the causative medicine, regardless of aetiology, including pituitary adenoma. Named dopamine agonists are bromocriptine, cabergoline and quinagolide.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.3.2 Primary Hypogonadism
document_sections.content: Substantial evidence does not support a spermatogenic benefit from gonadotrophins in classical testicular failure. Data also do not support SERMs, AIs or other hormonal therapies to improve spermatogenesis in primary hypogonadism.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.3.3 Idiopathic Male Factor Infertility
document_sections.content: Some evidence suggests that FSH improves semen measures in idiopathic oligozoospermia when FSH is normal, generally 1.5 – 8 mIU/mL. A meta-analysis of 12 trials and 924 patients reported improvements in semen parameters and SDF. Other reports suggest improvement in SDF, AMH and inhibin measures. Higher-dose FSH produced more testicular responses than lower doses. A Cochrane review of six RCTs involving 456 participants, with varied regimens and follow-up, found higher live-birth and pregnancy rates than with placebo or no treatment, but no significant group difference when ICSI or IUI was considered. A meta-analysis of 15 trials involving > 1,200 patients reported similar findings for spontaneous and post-ART pregnancy. One study of azoospermic men receiving TESE-ICSI reported higher sperm-retrieval, pregnancy and fertilisation rates with FSH than without it. Only one study found increased sperm-retrieval rates with combined hCG/FSH in NOA. hCG alone before TESE in NOA has not been found to improve sperm retrieval. Evidence for hormonal treatment before surgical sperm retrieval remains limited; it should be restricted to trials rather than used routinely.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.3.4 Anabolic Steroid Abuse
document_sections.content: Initial management of oligospermia or azoospermia following anabolic steroid abuse is withdrawal of the steroid. There is no uniform indication for additional treatment; available management draws on case reports and clinical experience. Sperm quantity and quality usually improve during the six to twelvemonth period following cessation. If impairment persists beyond that interval, hCG alone or with FSH may be used to stimulate spermatogenesis as an alternative to clomiphene.

document_sections.heading: 11.5.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for treatment of male infertility with hormonal therapy
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that FSH supports pubertal testicular growth and spermatogenesis, while hCG acts like LH to promote intratesticular testosterone and spermatogenesis after puberty in hypopituitarism (LE 2b). Prepubertal secondary hypogonadism requires FSH plus hCG or pulsatile GnRH, whose delivery is difficult (LE 1b). Subcutaneous hCG and FSH can effectively treat adult secondary hypogonadism (LE 2b). GnRH costs more and offers no advantage over gonadotropins in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (LE 3). For postpubertal secondary hypogonadism, sequential hCG then FSH or an initial combination are options (LE 1b); baseline testicular volume is an important response predictor (LE 2a). Dopamine agonists treat hyperprolactinaemia (LE 2a). FSH formulations have been associated with better sperm quality and higher spontaneous and assisted pregnancy rates in idiopathic infertility (LE 2a), but high-dose FSH before (m)TESE is not supported by conclusive evidence or routine-use recommendations (LE 2a). Testosterone treatment is contraindicated in infertile men (LE 1a). For men with congenital or acquired hypogonadotropic hypogonadism who want conception, the guideline recommends effective spermatogenesis-inducing treatment with hCG, human menopausal gonadotropins, recombinant FSH or highly purified FSH (Strong). It recommends FSH for idiopathic oligozoospermia with normal FSH to increase spermatogenesis (Weak), but advises against high-dose FSH for idiopathic infertility (Weak) and against stimulation before TESE in NOA outside trials (Weak). Testosterone must not be used to treat male infertility (Strong); it should be provided for symptomatic primary or secondary hypogonadism when parenthood is not being contemplated (Strong). Dopamine agonists may be offered for proven hyperprolactinemia to improve sperm quality (Weak). In infertile anabolic-steroid users, steroids should be stopped for six to twelve months before SERMs or gonadotrophins are considered (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 11.6 Invasive Male Infertility Management
document_sections.content: This part addresses diagnostic and surgical management of obstructive and non-obstructive azoospermia.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.1 Obstructive azoospermia
document_sections.content: Obstructive azoospermia (OA) denotes absence of sperm in centrifuged ejaculate sediment because of a blockage. It occurs in 20-40% of men with azoospermia and typically accompanies normal FSH, normal-sized testes and enlarged epididymides. Table 11.4 presents causes according to the location of obstruction.

document_sections.heading: Table 11.4: Causes of obstruction of the genitourinary system
document_sections.content: The table organises obstruction by intratesticular, epididymal, vas deferens and ejaculatory-duct sites, including infectious, traumatic, postsurgical, congenital, cystic and functional causes. Its site labels include Intratesticular (15%) and Epididymis (30-67%).

document_sections.heading: 11.6.1.1 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: History-taking follows the general male-infertility assessment. Potential obstructive causes include previous operations and injury during inguinal herniorrhaphy, orchidopexy or hydrocelectomy.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.1.1.1 Clinical examination
document_sections.content: Examination follows the general infertility assessment. OA is suggested by at least one testis measuring > 15 mL, although concomitant partial testicular failure may leave the testis smaller. Additional findings include epididymal enlargement or dilatation, epididymal or vas-deferens nodules, and absent or partly atretic vas deferens. Low or absent ejaculate volume warrants a search for sperm in post-ejaculatory urine. A semen pellet lacking both sperm and immature germ cells suggests complete seminal-duct obstruction.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.1.1.2 Hormone levels
document_sections.content: FSH and inhibin-B are expected to be normal in OA, but normal levels do not rule out other testicular causes of azoospermia, including NOA. Inhibin‐B reflects Sertoli-cell integrity and spermatogenesis but offers no better diagnostic value than FSH and is not widely advocated in practice.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.1.1.3 Genetic testing
document_sections.content: CFTR gene testing should be undertaken when the vas deferens is absent on one or both sides or when seminal vesicles are absent.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.1.1.4 Testicular biopsy
document_sections.content: A testicular biopsy, including FNA, should not be performed without simultaneous therapeutic sperm retrieval because it would necessitate another invasive procedure. Even profound spermatogenic failure, including SCOS, can contain focal spermatogenesis.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.1.2.1 Sperm retrieval
document_sections.content: For intratesticular obstruction, testicular sperm retrieval is recommended because no other retrieval site can provide sperm. With CBAVD-related epididymal obstruction, MESA or PESA is indicated; TESE and TESA are additional options. In OA treated with ICSI, studies of low evidentiary quality suggest that neither obstruction cause nor epididymal versus testicular sperm source changes pregnancy or miscarriage outcomes; pregnancy results also appear comparable with fresh and frozen–thawed epididymal sperm. One MESA procedure usually supplies sperm for several ICSI cycles and has yielded high fertilisation and pregnancy rates. For acquired epididymal obstruction when the female partner has good ovarian reserve, microsurgical EV is recommended. End-to-site and intussusception approaches are described. Recanalisation can require 3-18 months; a systematic review reported patency after 2.8 to 6.6 months and heterogeneous late-failure rates of 1 to 50%. At reconstruction, or whenever reconstruction cannot be performed, intra-operative MESA/TESE retrieval with cryopreservation should be undertaken for later ICSI. Reported patency rates are 63% to 85%, and cumulative natural-pregnancy rates are 21% to 45%. Bilateral EV and targeting the caudal or corpus epididymis when feasible might improve patency; operative findings may adversely affect success, and robot-assisted EV needs larger studies despite similar reported success. Post-vasectomy vas obstruction requires microsurgical reversal: sample-size-weighted mean patency and pregnancy rates were 90-97% and 52-73%, time to patency averaged 1.7-4.3 months, and late failure occurred in 0-12%. Robot-assisted vasovasostomy has similar reported success, but its benefit over standard microsurgery needs larger studies and cost-benefit assessment. No sperm in intra-operative vas fluid, particularly thick “toothpaste” fluid proximally, suggests secondary epididymal obstruction and may indicate EV; concurrent retrieval for ICSI cryopreservation may be performed after counselling. Large bilateral inguinal vas defects from earlier hernia surgery or orchidopexy usually cannot be reconstructed; TESE/MESA/ PESA or proximal vas aspiration can provide sperm for freezing and later ICSI. Management of EDO depends on cause: TURED may treat post-inflammatory or cystic obstruction, while a midline intraprostatic cyst requires incision, unroofing or aspiration. TURED can remove part of the verumontanum; reported pregnancy rates are 20-25%. Its complications include epididymitis, UTI, visible haematuria, haematospermia, azoospermia with partial distal obstruction, and urinary reflux into ejaculatory ducts and seminal vesicles. Other approaches include seminal vesiculoscopy to clear material or stones, balloon dilation, laser incision for calcification identified on TRUS, MESA, PESA, TESA, TESE, proximal vas aspiration and ultrasound-guided seminal-vesicle aspiration.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.1.3 Summary of evidence and recommendations for obstructive azoospermia
document_sections.content: Seminal-tract obstruction is common with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia and generally accompanies normal testicular size and reproductive hormones (LE 3). For vasal or epididymal obstruction and a female partner with good ovarian reserve, microsurgical vasovasostomy or epididymovasostomy is recommended (Strong). MESA, TESE, PESA or TESA should be used alongside reconstruction, for obstruction unsuitable for repair, when the partner's ovarian reserve is limited, or when the couple prefers ICSI without reconstruction (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 11.6.2 Non-obstructive azoospermia
document_sections.content: NOA is absence of sperm from the centrifuged ejaculate despite usually normal ejaculate volume. At least two consecutive semen analyses should confirm azoospermia. The marked spermatogenic deficit often reflects primary testicular dysfunction but can instead involve the hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.2.1 Investigation of non-obstructive azoospermia
document_sections.content: History and examination follow the general male-infertility work-up. NOA can initially reveal a pituitary tumour or testicular germ-cell tumour. Patients have increased risks of long-term cardio-metabolic disease, cancer and mortality, making assessment an opportunity for broader risk stratification. Comprehensive hormonal tests and scrotal US are important. About 30% have concomitant hypogonadism; biochemical assessment should distinguish hypogonadotropic, hypergonadotropic and compensated forms because treatment differs. Scrotal US can reveal inhomogeneous architecture, microcalcifications or uncommon testicular tumours. Testicular volume is often, but not invariably, low and may indicate spermatogenic function. Evidence on whether Doppler perfusion predicts TESE retrieval or usefully guides biopsy is inconsistent and does not support routine pre-TESE Doppler prediction. Karyotyping and Y-chromosome micro-deletion screening should be undertaken; suspected CBAVD also warrants CFTR mutation assessment. Couples should receive counselling concerning potentially transmissible or health-relevant genetic findings.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.2.2 Surgery for non-obstructive azoospermia
document_sections.content: Surgery aims to obtain viable sperm directly from one or both testes, usually for IVF with ICSI. A preliminary testicular biopsy before TESE is not recommended.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.2.3 Indications and techniques of sperm retrieval
document_sections.content: Spermatogenesis can persist in isolated testicular foci. Across heterogeneous cohorts and procedures, positive sperm-retrieval rates have reached up to 50% in NOA, but no definitive preoperative predictor has been established. Hypospermatogenesis on biopsy predicted retrieval after TESE more accurately than maturation arrest or SCOS in cited studies. Associations of FSH, LH, inhibin B, AMH and testicular volume with retrieval have been variable or disputed. Complete AZFa and AZFb deletions make successful retrieval almost impossible, so TESE is contraindicated. Patients with Klinefelter syndrome or previously undescended testes have shown better surgical retrieval prospects. Predictive machine-learning approaches are emerging but remain prospective tools.

document_sections.heading: Fine needle aspiration mapping
document_sections.content: FNA mapping has been proposed to identify NOA candidates and testicular sites for subsequent TESE and ICSI through cytological and histological examination. A positive map still requires therapeutic surgery and may add testicular-damage risk. Without a suitable cost-benefit analysis this additional procedure is unjustified. Salvage mTESE after mapping has not been studied, and FNA mapping is not recommended as primary therapy pending further RCTs.

document_sections.heading: Testicular sperm aspiration
document_sections.content: TESA obtains testicular tissue with a biopsy needle under local anaesthesia in an office setting. Reported retrieval rates span 11 to 60% according to patient and technique. Complications are uncommon, chiefly minor bleeding, scrotal haematoma and postoperative pain. A meta-analysis of case-control studies found TESE two times (95% CI: 1.8-2.2) more likely than TESA to retrieve sperm. Because success is lower than with TESE, TESA is no longer recommended for NOA.

document_sections.heading: Conventional and mTESE
document_sections.content: Conventional TESE uses a scrotal incision and open testicular biopsy; single-arm studies report retrieval around 50%, and observational work suggests that multiple biopsies improve the chance of retrieval. It has been associated with more complications: scrotal US found intratesticular haematoma in 51.7% at 3 months and fibrosis in up to 30% at 6-months’ assessment, although the longer-term functional implications remain uncertain. mTESE uses an operative microscope at 20-25x to select larger, dilated, opaque seminiferous tubules, aiming to retrieve sperm with less sampled tissue and fewer complications. Haematoma and fibrosis have been less frequent than after cTESE; baseline testosterone has recovered after long-term follow-up with both techniques, making longer-term endocrine follow-up reasonable after either TESE approach. A case-control-study meta-analysis reported unadjusted retrieval rates of 35% (95% CI: 30-40) with TESE versus 52% (95% CI: 47-58) with mTESE. Another meta-analysis found overall retrieval of 47% (95% CI: 45;49%) and no difference between cTESE, 46 [range 43-49] %, and mTESE, 46 [range 42-49] %. Its meta-regression found no relation to age or enrolment hormone levels but increasing retrieval with greater testicular volume. Retrieved sperm resulted in live birth of up to 28% per ICSI cycle. The meta-analyses differed in included study designs, yet individual direct comparisons favoured mTESE. In SCOS, reported rates were 22.5 to 41% for mTESE versus 6.3 to 29% for cTESE; maturation arrest showed no technique difference, and one study found a small mTESE advantage in hypospermatogenesis. Salvage mTESE yielded sperm in 46.5% in one study after failed cTESE or TESA; other post-TESE or post-cTESE reports gave 39.1% (range 18.4-57.1%). Retrospective, limited studies suggest hypospermatogenesis might predict salvage success. Following failed mTESE, reported salvage rates ranged from 18.4% to 42.8%. A meta-analysis found that total testosterone in NOA fell by a mean 2.7 nmol/L at 6 months after cTESE and returned to baseline within 18-26 months. In the only cited RCT, involving 100 men, mTESE retrieved sperm more often than multiple-pass 18G needle TESA (43% vs. 22%; rate difference -0.21; 95% Cl -0.39 to – 0.03; p = 0.02). Adding salvage mTESE after unsuccessful TESA yielded combined retrieval of 29%, not significantly different from mTESE alone, but the trial lacked power for that comparison. Evidence is limited by observational designs, variable diagnoses, techniques and outcome reporting, and few RCTs directly compare cTESE with mTESE. Despite no overall difference in the most comprehensive meta-analysis, direct trials favoured mTESE, and available data suggest fewer complications. The panel therefore considers mTESE optimal by consensus, while acknowledging low-quality evidence and a need for larger RCTs reporting retrieval, harms, costs, procedural details, sperm characteristics and ART live births.

document_sections.heading: Hormonal therapy prior to surgical sperm retrieval approaches
document_sections.content: Increasing intratesticular testosterone or FSH to improve sperm retrieval in NOA has been proposed using hCG, FSH or SERMs, without a standard protocol. No RCT has demonstrated improved retrieval following hormonal treatment in idiopathic NOA. A meta-analysis suggested possible benefit before TESE for eugonadal but not hypergonadotropic hypogonadal patients; its studies had moderate or severe bias risk, requiring randomised confirmation. Small retrospective studies of hormonal preparation for salvage surgery after failed cTESE or mTESE conflict; hypospermatogenesis emerged as a possible predictor in one context. Patients should be advised that supporting evidence is limited, and hormonal preparation is not currently recommended routinely.

document_sections.heading: 11.6.2.4 Recommendations for Non-Obstructive Azoospermia
document_sections.content: The evidence summary links NOA to later cardio-metabolic disease, cancer and death (LE 3) and reports hypogonadism in about one third before sperm-retrieval surgery (LE 3). Surgical sperm retrieval is necessary before ART in NOA (LE 1b). FNA and TESA retrieve sperm less often than TESE (LE 1b); FNA also entails another potentially damaging procedure without demonstrated cost-benefit justification (LE 2a). No reliable definitive pre-TESE retrieval predictors have been found (LE 1b). mTESE has been associated with more retrieval and fewer complications than conventional TESE (LE 2a). Evidence remains inconclusive for medication before TESE, including rFSH, highly purified FSH, hCG, AIs or SERMs (LE 2a). The guideline requires confirmation of NOA by two consecutive semen analyses showing no sperm after centrifugation (Strong). It recommends detailed history, hormonal profile, genetic testing and scrotal US to investigate cause and comorbidity (Strong), and requires genetic counselling before ART when a couple has a genetic abnormality (Strong). Sperm-retrieval surgery should be performed for ART candidates (Strong), but not with complete AZFa and AZFb deletions (Strong). FNA and TESA should not be used in NOA (Strong), nor should prognostic FNA mapping precede definitive testicular extraction (Weak). mTESE is the preferred retrieval treatment (Weak). Preoperative clinical or biochemical variables should not be treated as sufficient, reliable predictors (Weak). Routine medical or hormonal stimulation before c/mTESE is discouraged in NOA with hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 11.7 Assisted Reproductive Technologies
document_sections.content: ART involves handling human oocytes and sperm, or embryos, in vitro with the aim of pregnancy. Appendix 7 contains a limited account of ART and safety.

document_sections.heading: 11.8 Psychosocial aspects in men’s infertility
document_sections.content: Male infertility can cause emotional distress and challenge identity. Unsuccessful treatment can lead to prolonged grief requiring psychological support afterwards. A mental-health professional is considered part of the infertility team throughout care, with interventions ranging from psycho-education to broader psychotherapy. Prevention also merits attention: men want parenthood but often know little about infertility risks or age-related fertility decline and may overestimate spontaneous-conception prospects.

document_sections.heading: 12. LATE EFFECTS, SURVIVORSHIP AND MEN’S HEALTH
document_sections.content: The EAU Guidelines Panel of Sexual and Reproductive Health reviewed later sexual and reproductive consequences of urological disease arising in childhood or adulthood, long-term cancer effects, and approaches to personalised male-health promotion. Searches of English-language original and review publications through December 2019, updated through December 2020 using Pubmed and Google, found limited literature on professional support for cancer survivors' sexual and reproductive health or Men's Health programmes. The panel notes a continuing life-expectancy gap between men and women. Important contributors to male mortality in Europe include non-communicable conditions, particularly CVDs, cancer, diabetes and respiratory disease, as well as injuries; a WHO report challenges the idea that excess premature male mortality is inevitable. COVID-19 further illustrates the importance of male-health strategies. The WHO report also identifies male sexual and reproductive health as under-reported and relates infertility, as a marker of general health, to serious disease. The panel calls for preventive care and follow-up of sexual or reproductive complaints rather than assuming mortality risks are simply attributable to failure to become a father. It encourages clinicians to consider associated health conditions: men diagnosed with varicoceles have higher heart-disease incidence and later diabetes and hyperlipidaemia risk. Infertility can also cause anxiety, persistent sadness, anger and feelings of inadequacy in men and partners; coping varies with personality, sociocultural circumstances, treatment and professional support. PCa is the most common cancer among European men when non-melanoma skin cancer is excluded. Improved survival makes quality of life and sexual well-being increasingly important; sexual dysfunction and distress are common following treatment regardless of modality. Fertility-preservation needs among cancer survivors remain poorly understood. Psychological effects of PCa may persist after remission or cure and restoration of erectile function. Gay and bisexual men with PCa have particular sexual concerns affected by heteronormative standards that can impair care quality, supporting a role for urologists in survivorship programmes. The association of ED with heart disease is well established. CVD leads male mortality and premature mortality, and major risks including hypertension, smoking and high cholesterol are more prevalent among men than women. As ED is an early sign of atherosclerotic disease and independently predicts cardiovascular events, its assessment offers an opportunity to screen and modify CVD risks. EAU and AUA guidelines recommend CVD-risk screening in men with ED and late-onset hypogonadism. The panel calls for prospective data across men's health, including CVD-screening protocols and assessments of primary and secondary prevention, and seeks a long-term global male-health strategy.
